heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.0 Philosophy
content:
The word "event" is a clinical term. Patients have cardiac events. Healthy users have **notable moments** — moments in their heart's day that are worth noticing, not because something is wrong, but because the heart did something interesting.

**Every notable moment is an observation, never a warning.** The app should not "alert" or "warn." It should say "here's something your heart did today." Some moments are about effort or achievement (a new HR peak, a strong recovery after exercise). Others are about rhythm (a cluster of early beats, a pause). Others are about adaptation (HRV rebounding above baseline, a heart settling unusually well after exertion). The framing matters more than the detection rule.

This reframing is grounded in how leading consumer health products work: WHOOP doesn't warn — it recommends ("green = go hard today"). Fitbit doesn't alert — it celebrates ("new personal best"). The research on consumer wearable engagement consistently finds that users respond better to validating, growth-framing language than to diagnostic language ["The More You Give the Wearable, the More It Gives You", Springer 2025].

**Three categories of notable moments:**

| Category | What it means | Tone |
|---|---|---|
| **Effort / achievement** | The heart performed at a level outside its usual range for this context — higher peak, deeper rest, stronger recovery | "Your heart did something worth noting" — neutral, factual, can be celebrated |
| **Rhythm / pattern** | The heart's beat-to-beat pattern showed something different — ectopic cluster, pause, rate surge/drop, alternating beats | "A different rhythm pattern appeared briefly" — observational, not diagnostic |
| **Adaptation / recovery** | The heart showed a recovery response that is different from usual — faster return to baseline, HRV overshoot, strong vagal rebound | "Your body responded [faster/slower] than it usually does" — informative about fitness and resilience |

Every `baseline.*_{context}` reference below is keyed by the **composite context class** (`{time_of_day}-{day_type}-{rhythm}-{motion}`, `04` §1.2), not the old three-bin motion class. Moment copy may cite the friendly class label (e.g. "your usual range for *morning · weekday · light-moderate · sedentary*") and, where present, the window's tags (`recovery`, `elevated`, `challenge_window` — `04` §1.2). The `challenge_window` tag is exactly the §3.3.1 step-1 challenge condition, and the `recovery` tag is the §3.3.1 step-3 rebound condition, so moment detection and window tagging stay in one definition.

heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.1 Effort and achievement moments
content:
These capture when the heart reaches levels outside its personal range for the current context. They are not "highs" or "lows" to be concerned about — they are peaks and depths worth knowing about.

| Moment | Detection rule | Framing |
|---|---|---|
| `hr_peak` | 5+ consecutive beats with instant HR > `baseline.hr_p95_{context}` | "Heart rate peaked at [X] bpm — outside your usual range for this kind of activity" |
| `hr_deep_rest` | 5+ consecutive beats with instant HR < `baseline.hr_p05_{context}`, not during detected sleep | "Heart rate settled to [X] bpm — unusually low for this context" |
| `hrv_peak` | Window RMSSD > `baseline.rmssd_p90_{context}` | "HRV reached [X] ms — above your usual range for this kind of window" |
| `dc_peak` | Window DC > `baseline.dc_p90_{context}` | "Vagal tone (heart's calming signal) was unusually strong during this window" |
| `hr_sustained_new_peak` | 30+ consecutive seconds with mean HR > any prior window of this context class in the past 90 days | "This was your highest sustained heart rate in this kind of activity — a new personal benchmark" |
| `edr_low` | Window EDR rate < `baseline.edr_p05_{context}`, not during sleep | "Breathing rate dropped to [X] breaths/min — unusually slow for this context" |

**Why personal-bests matter**: WHOOP highlights "strain" as an achievement. Fitbit uses "heart rate zones" as milestones. A user who hits a new HR peak during exercise is experiencing cardiovascular adaptation — their body is capable of a level it wasn't before. That is worth marking, whether they're an athlete or someone who just took the stairs for the first time in months.

heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.2 Rhythm and pattern moments
content:
These capture when the beat-to-beat rhythm shows something different from the usual pattern. They are neutral observations, not warnings.

| Moment | Detection rule | Framing |
|---|---|---|
| `ectopic_cluster` | 3+ PVCs or PACs within 10 consecutive beats | "A brief cluster of early beats — [N] in [M] beats" |
| `bigeminy` | Alternating normal-ectopic pattern for 6+ beats | "An alternating beat pattern appeared briefly" |
| `trigeminy` | Normal-normal-ectopic pattern for 9+ beats | "A pattern of early beats every third beat — brief" |
| `pause` | RR > 2000 ms (single RR) OR RR > 150% of mean RR over last 20 beats AND RR > 1500 ms | "A pause between beats: [X] ms — about [Y]× longer than your usual rhythm" |
| `hr_surge` | HR increases by > 20 bpm over 30 s, sustained for 60+ s | "Heart rate rose quickly — from [X] to [Y] bpm over about 30 seconds" |
| `hr_drop` | HR drops by > 20 bpm over 30 s, sustained for 60+ s (not at sleep onset) | "Heart rate dropped quickly — from [X] to [Y] bpm" |
| `hr_coupling_jump` | HR change (≥ 20 bpm within 60 s) coincides with a **sustained** motion spike (motion_centroid > 3× previous, held ≥ 3 consecutive beats); one moment per consolidated HR-shift event | "Heart rate shifted with movement" — contextualizes the rate change |
| `twa_notable` | `twa_max ≥ 60 μV` in any 15 s sub-window | "T-wave variation was more pronounced than usual" — only surfaces if sustained across multiple days |

**Implemented 2026-08-15 (consolidation + sustained-motion gate, `dataset-tooling/analysis/moments.py`).** The initial implementation emitted one `hr_coupling_jump` per qualifying beat pair with no sustained-motion requirement, which produced 170 moments on the cross-session recording (a session with real motion) vs 4 on sedentary `micahz`. The rule now clusters consecutive qualifying pairs (start times within `COUPLING_CLUSTER_S` = 60 s) into one HR-shift event and emits exactly one moment per event (duration spans the cluster; `hr_delta` = max Δ; `motion_mg` = max sustained motion); a single-beat >3× motion spike no longer fires (motion must stay elevated ≥ `MOTION_SUSTAIN_BEATS` = 3 beats above the pre-jump baseline), and the ±30 s motion proximity window is kept (`MOTION_PROXIMITY_S`). Re-run: cross-session 170 → 43 (per-window 0.38, down from ~1.5), `micahz` 4 → 2.

heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.3 Adaptation and recovery moments
content: These capture how the heart responds to preceding activity. They are among the most interesting cardiac events for a longitudinal app because they reveal the body's adaptive capacity — fitness, stress, resilience.

heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.3 Adaptation and recovery moments > 3.3.1 Vagal rebound (parasympathetic overshoot)
content:
After intense exercise or any high-HR window, the parasympathetic nervous system reactivates. In well-adapted individuals, this reactivation is strong and fast — HR drops below baseline and HRV rises above baseline. This is called vagal rebound [PMC2886688, Frontiers Physiology 10.3389/fphys.2025.1579929] and is a positive marker of cardiovascular fitness and autonomic health.

**Detection rule**:
```
1. Identify a "challenge" window: hr_mean > baseline.hr_p80_{context} OR motion_centroid > 100 mG sustained for > 5 minutes
2. Look at the immediate next window (within 15 minutes of the challenge window ending)
3. If next_window.hr_mean < baseline.hr_p20_{context} AND next_window.rmssd > baseline.rmssd_p80_{context}:
    moment_type = "vagal_rebound"
    detail = "Heart rate settled below usual resting for this context, and HRV rose above your typical range — a strong recovery response"
```

heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.3 Adaptation and recovery moments > 3.3.2 Recovery speed change
content:
Over time, the app learns how long it typically takes the user to return to baseline after a high-exertion window. When this time changes significantly, it's a notable moment — faster recovery means improved fitness, slower recovery means accumulated strain.

**Detection rule**:
```
Compare current_recovery_minutes to baseline.recovery_minutes_{context_class}:
    if current < baseline.p20:
        moment_type = "faster_recovery"
        detail = "Your heart returned to resting rhythm faster than usual after activity — [X] minutes vs your typical [Y]"
    if current > baseline.p80:
        moment_type = "slower_recovery"
        detail = "Your heart took longer than usual to settle after activity — [X] minutes vs your typical [Y]. This can happen after bigger days, less sleep, or accumulated fatigue."
```

heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.3 Adaptation and recovery moments > 3.3.3 Overnight HRV rebound
content:
After a day with multiple high-exertion windows (or a user-tagged "big day"), the overnight HRV can rise above baseline — the body is rebuilding, and this is a positive signal [IJERPH 10.3390/ijerph19169797].

**Detection rule**:
```
if (day had 3+ high_exertion windows OR user tagged "big day" / "workout" / "race") AND 
   overnight_window.rmssd > baseline.rmssd_p80_{sleep_context}:
    moment_type = "overnight_rebound"
    detail = "After active windows earlier today, your overnight HRV rose above your usual range — your body is rebuilding. This is a sign that your cardiovascular system is responding well to exertion."
```

heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.3 Adaptation and recovery moments > 3.3.4 Settling acceleration
content:
Heart rate deceleration at sleep onset (how quickly HR drops when the user falls asleep) changes with fatigue, stress, and fitness. A notably fast or slow settling is worth marking.

**Detection rule**:
```
Compute hr_settling_slope = (HR at sleep onset - HR 30 minutes later) / 30
if |hr_settling_slope - baseline.settling_slope| > 2 * baseline.settling_slope_mad:
    moment_type = "settling_fast" or "settling_slow"
    detail = "Your heart settled [faster/slower] than usual at the start of rest tonight"
```

heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.4 Window moment summary
Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.5 Notability tiers
content:
"Severity" is a clinical term. "Notability" describes how much a moment stands out from the user's usual pattern.

| Tier | Criteria | User language |
|---|---|---|
| `noticed` | Single moment, within 2× baseline range, brief | Included in the window's detail, but not highlighted on the timeline card |
| `interesting` | Sustained moment, multiple moments in one window, beyond 2× baseline range, or any adaptation/recovery moment | Appears on the timeline card for the window — a small marker that says "something to see here" |
| `significant` | Multiple windows in a day with interesting moments, OR a moment beyond 3× baseline range, OR a personal-best moment (new HR/HRV peak in 90+ days) | Surfaces as a line item in the daily summary's "notable moments" section |

**Key framing principle**: `interesting` and `significant` are invitations to look, not warnings to fear. A `significant` vagal rebound is good news. A `significant` HR peak is an achievement. A `significant` pause merits context — the user may want to know it happened, but the app does not tell them to worry.

heading_path: Window notable moments > 3. Notable Moments (formerly "Events") > 3.5 Notability tiers
content:
**Implemented 2026-08-13 (T9, `dataset-tooling/analysis/moments.py`).** The §3.1–3.3 rules are implemented offline behind a pluggable `Baseline`; the real pass uses a within-session self-baseline (production replaces it with 90 days of context-conditioned data). Measured behavior on `micahz`:
- Beat-level rules (hr_peak/deep_rest, ectopic_cluster, bigeminy/trigeminy, pause, surge/drop) run **only on beats with `sqi in [good, fair]`** (the §2 inclusion rule). Running them on all beats let the degraded late-session signal emit 217 ectopic_cluster moments; with the filter, 75.
- `ectopic_cluster` counts inherit the T6 classifier's relative-prematurity definition (`rr < 0.80 × the rate-adaptive reference RR`, the median of the last 10 non-artifact RRs — spec §1.3, revised 2026-08-14). The old last-10-*normal*-mean reference lags during a genuine rate transition (e.g. RR 1200→820 ms over ~60 s at good SQI), labeling a run of beats as ectopic; the adaptive median resolves the cascade (cross-session ectopic 4.22% → 1.35%, `ectopic_cluster` 213 → 3). The **2026-08-15 run-resolution pass** (§1.3) then reclassifies the residual premature runs by post-run context (compensatory pause / refractory re-trigger), calibrated to 44/45 agreement on the 50 hand-labeled runs: cross-session ectopic 1.35% → 0.45% (`ectopic_cluster` 3 → 0), `micahz` 0.10% → 0.01% (`ectopic_cluster` 15 → 1).
- `twa_notable` fires on the 15 s MMA sub-window max; on `micahz` that max reaches 200–735 µV on isolated high-HR/noise bins while the window's `twa_median` stays <10 µV. Per the §2.3.1 caveat (single-day spikes suppressed; multi-day trend required) a single window's `twa_notable` is reported at the `noticed` tier only.
- Adaptation/recovery moments (vagal_rebound, recovery speed, overnight/settling) need a challenge→next-window pairing and sleep context; on the 68-window `micahz` pass no window pair met the rebound conditions (0 adaptation/recovery moments).

heading_path: Window notable moments > 4. ECG-Derived Respiration (EDR)
content:
Respiration modulates heart rate (respiratory sinus arrhythmia) and QRS amplitude (chest impedance changes with breathing). From a chest-strap single-lead ECG, two EDR signals can be extracted:

1. **RSA-based EDR**: The high-frequency component of RR interval variation (peak-to-peak modulation in the 0.15-0.40 Hz band, ~9-24 breaths/min). Extracted via bandpass filter on the RR interval series.
2. **Amplitude-based EDR**: The beat-to-beat modulation of R-wave amplitude caused by chest expansion/contraction during breathing. Extracted from the `r_amp_uv` time series.

Both signals are bandpass filtered (0.1-0.5 Hz, corresponding to 6-30 breaths/min). The dominant frequency in each is estimated via zero-crossing rate. The two estimates are averaged when both are available; if only one is available, that one is used.

Window-level EDR metrics:

| Metric | Computation |
|---|---|
| `edr_rate` | Median breathing rate over the window (breaths/min) |
| `edr_variability` | IQR of breathing rate within the window |
| `edr_quality` | `good` (both signals agree within 3 bpm), `fair` (one signal only or modest disagreement), `poor` (large disagreement or high noise) |

EDR is a secondary metric. It augments the heart analysis but is not used for clinical interpretation or flags. It is particularly useful for sleep-window analysis (slow, regular breathing is a sleep indicator).

heading_path: Window notable moments > 5. Data Quality Gates Per Window
content:
Before emitting window metrics to the timeline, a quality gate assesses whether the window has enough data:

| Gate | Threshold | Action on failure |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum beats | 30 valid (non-artifact) beats | Window stored with most metrics `null`; `quality = "sparse"` |
| Minimum SQI | `sqi_fraction_good > 0.33` (at least 1/3 of window in good SQI) | Window stored with `quality = "degraded"`; HRV/morphology suppressed |
| Ectopic contamination | `ectopic_fraction < 0.30` (trailing 5-min window) | HRV metrics flagged `high_ectopic_period` but still computed (ectopics already excluded) |
| Gap contamination | Window contains > 10% gap-filled beats | Window `quality = "gap_compromised"`; only HR mean reported |

The quality gate is permissive by design — it is better to report what can be reported with a quality caveat than to delete windows. The longitudinal analytics layer will weigh windows by their quality when computing baselines.

**Implemented 2026-08-13 (T8, `dataset-tooling/analysis/window_metrics.py`).** The §2 metric set is implemented offline over `segment_with_gaps` context windows (not fixed 5-min buckets). Measured behavior on `micahz` (34,646 beats, 68 windows median 236 s):
- The spec's triangulation formula (`pr_median + qrs_median + (qt_median - qrs_median) > qt_median + 30 ms`) algebraically degenerates to `pr_median > 30 ms`, which is always true — it is reported as `triangulation_overlap_ms` for inspection, not applied as a gate.
- HRV needs ≥30 NN RRs and PRSA ≥120, so the shortest context windows (62–90 s) report `null` HRV/DC — 63% of `micahz` windows have DC, 93% have HRV.
- EDR `edr_variability` is `null` in this port (one dominant-rate estimate per window); `edr_quality` still reports the RSA-vs-amplitude agreement.
- PR appears in morphology medians; the T2 caveat (P-metrics excluded from automated flags until the on-device 500 Hz path lands) applies to flags, not display medians.
- Rhythm fractions use the window's full beat count as denominator so every fraction is in [0, 1].

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > Overview
content:
This document defines how heart metrics are tracked over days, weeks, and months to build personal baselines, detect trends, surface gentle check-in flags, and detect sleep/circadian patterns. Every analysis is designed for the consumer wellness user — language is cautious, comparisons are within-person, and flags are gentle.

This document extends and specializes the project's broader longitudinal research (`../legacy/research/001-longitudinal-physiological-analysis/`) to the ECG-specific metrics available from the H10 signal pipeline.

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 1. The Baseline Model > 1.1 Why context-conditioned baselines
content: The existing research establishes that wearable physiology is highly individual and that personal baselines are more useful than population norms [S07, S11, S12]. The Heart Analysis Approach extends this: baselines are conditioned on **context class**, because a resting heart rate of 65 during sleep is normal, while the same rate during a walking window might be unusually low.

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 1. The Baseline Model > 1.2 Context classes for baseline grouping
content:
Window context descriptors are quantized into a **composite context class** used as the baseline key everywhere the old three-bin class (`still`/`active`/`high_motion`) was used: baseline primary key, moment priors, body-load bands, UI labels, and the Supabase `context_windows.context_class` column. The composite key is:

```
class_key = "{time_of_day}-{day_type}-{rhythm}-{motion}"
e.g. "morning-weekday-light_moderate-sedentary"
```

| Dimension | Binning strategy | Resulting bins |
|---|---|---|
| `time_of_day` | 8 fixed wall-clock bins | `night` 00–05, `early_morning` 05–08, `morning` 08–11, `late_morning` 11–13, `early_afternoon` 13–16, `afternoon` 16–19, `evening` 19–22, `late_night` 22–24 |
| `day_type` | Categorical from wall-clock day of week | `weekday`, `weekend` |
| `rhythm` | **Self-calibrating quintiles** (p20/p40/p60/p80) of the user's own window `hr_median` stream, read from the global HR t-digest in `StreamingBaseline` — thresholds come from the user's *prior* windows (causal; classified before the window updates the baseline), seeded from the population prior (75 ± 15 bpm) on cold start | `light`, `light_moderate`, `moderate`, `moderate_vigorous`, `vigorous` |
| `motion` | Absolute thresholds (not self-calibrated) + sleep score | `sleeping` (via the §4.1 sleep score where available, else a conservative heuristic), `sedentary` (< 20 mG), `active` (≥ 20 mG) |

There are up to 8 × 2 × 5 × 3 = 240 possible classes, but most users populate only **20–40** regularly due to natural routine. Sparse classes are handled by the empirical-Bayes shrinkage below — they borrow strength from the cross-context prior rather than waiting for a minimum window count.

**Tags** are per-window metadata that ride alongside the class but are **not part of the baseline key**:

| Tag | Condition |
|---|---|
| `is_waking` | Window's motion bin is not `sleeping` |
| `recovery` | Window `hr_median` below the class p20 **AND** window RMSSD above the class p80 (heart settled unusually low with strong HRV) |
| `elevated` | Window `hr_median` above the class p80 |
| `challenge_window` | Reuses the `03` §3.3.1 challenge definition: `hr_mean` above the class p80 OR motion > 100 mG sustained for > 5 min |

Tags are persisted on the window, shown in the UI, and used by moment copy; they never affect which baseline a window updates.

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 1. The Baseline Model > 1.3 Baseline computation
content:
For each metric (e.g., `hr_mean`, `rmssd`, `dc`, `qrs_median`) and each context class, a **streaming, tiered baseline** is maintained. It replaces the old "wait for 14–30 windows per context class before anything is reportable" gate with an incremental model that starts producing a usable (honestly-uncertain) band from the first valid window and tightens as data accumulates (decisions log 2026-08-15; prototype `dataset-tooling/analysis/baseline.py`, validated by T10).

**Streaming sufficient statistics.** Every closing `quality = good` window updates per-context-class sufficient statistics — O(1) memory, no batch re-scan:

- window count `n`, sum, sum-of-squares (→ mean, variance),
- EWMA with `alpha = 0.05` for slow drift (unchanged from the prior model),
- a t-digest [S30] for streaming p05/p10/p20/p80/p90/p95 "usual range" percentiles.

**Empirical-Bayes (James–Stein) shrinkage.** A sparse context class borrows strength from a cross-context prior (the user's overall distribution per metric family; population priors from research cover day zero):

```python
theta_j = (1 - B_j) * class_mean_j + B_j * prior_mean
B_j     = (sigma2 / n_j) / (tau2 + sigma2 / n_j)
```

where `sigma2` is the within-class variance, `tau2` the between-class variance, and `n_j` the class window count. A class with few windows is pulled toward the prior (`B_j -> 1`); a well-populated class keeps its own mean (`B_j -> 0`).

**Small-sample band correction.** The deviation Z-score statistic follows a Student-t with `n - 1` degrees of freedom [S31], so early percentile bands are scaled by `t(n-1, 1-alpha) / z(1-alpha)`. Bands start wide but honest and converge to the raw percentile band as `n` grows.

**Confidence tiers.** The binary reportable / not-reportable gate is replaced by three tiers that surface in the UI as transparent uncertainty (design principle "Transparent uncertainty"):

| Tier | Condition | UI treatment |
|---|---|---|
| `learning` | `n < 5` | "Still learning this context — wide range." Estimates exist but are marked low-confidence; the band is dominated by the prior and the Student-t widening. |
| `establishing` | `5 <= n < established_n` | "Building a picture — ranges tightening." Usable band; flags only at high thresholds. |
| `established` | `n >= established_n` | Full confidence. Standard band + robust-z display. |

**Established levels** (per metric family — these are the old "minimum windows" values, now the point where the tier becomes `established` rather than a hard gate):

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 1. The Baseline Model > 1.3 Baseline computation
content:
| Metric Family | `established_n` | Deviation Display |
|---|---|---|
| HR mean | 14 | Robust z-score and percentile band |
| RMSSD / SDNN | 21 | Robust z-score |
| DC (deceleration capacity) | 21 | Percentile band (lower DC = noteworthy) |
| QRS duration | 30 | Robust z-score |
| QTc | 30 | Robust z-score (single-lead QTc has limited validity) |
| Tp-e | 30 | Robust z-score (within-person trend; single-lead Tp-e is lead-dependent) |
| TWA (max) | 30 | Absolute threshold + robust z-score (47/60 μV) |
| ST level | 30 | Robust z-score (trend-based; >100 μV deviation from personal baseline is notable) |
| QT-RR slope | 30 | Robust z-score (flatter or steeper adaptation vs personal norm) |
| QRS-T area ratio | 30 | Robust z-score (within-person shifts in repolarization balance) |
| EDR rate | 14 | Robust z-score |
| Ectopic fraction | 30 | Percentile band (higher = noteworthy) |

**Baseline quality gating** (unchanged):

- Only windows with `quality = good` (not `sparse`, `degraded`, `gap_compromised`) contribute to baseline updates.
- After user-tagged unusual periods (illness, travel, medication change, heavy event like marathon), a 2-3 day "cooldown" period pauses baseline updates per personal-baselines.md recommendation.
- Data from gap-filled periods (`gap_filled_rr`) does NOT update baselines (no context, no morphology, reduced trust in RR-only data).

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 1. The Baseline Model > 1.4 Robust deviation score
content:
For any window metric value `x` and its context-class baseline, the deviation score uses the shrunken center `theta` and the (Student-t widened) band:

```python
robust_z = 0.6745 * (x - theta) / band_sd
```

where `band_sd = (p90 - p10) / (2 * z_0.90)` for the shrunken, widened band. In the `learning` tier the widened band keeps the false-positive rate at the nominal level (T10 synthetic pass: early false-flag rate 0.209 vs nominal 0.20) — a value inside a wide early band is genuinely "too little data to tell."

Interpretation scale:

| |robust_z| | User-facing band | Language |
|---|---|---|---|
| < 1.0 | "within usual range" | "Your heart rate was in your normal range for this kind of activity." |
| 1.0 – 2.0 | "slightly outside" | "A bit outside your usual range for this context." |
| 2.0 – 3.0 | "outside usual range" | "Your heart rate was higher/lower than usual for this context." |
| > 3.0 | "well outside" | "Notably higher/lower than your typical pattern for this context." |

In `learning`/`establishing` tiers the same |robust_z| values carry a confidence qualifier ("based on limited data so far").

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 2. Trend Cards > 2.1 Trend metrics
content:
| Trend | Computation | Update cadence | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **7-day HR trend** | Linear slope of daily `hr_mean` (overnight windows only, or resting windows if sleep detection unavailable) over last 7 days | Daily | Direction and magnitude of resting HR change |
| **28-day HR trend** | Linear slope over last 28 days | Every 3 days | Longer-term cardio trend |
| **HRV trend** | 7-day median RMSSD vs 60-day baseline median | Daily | "Recovery signal trending below/above usual" per recovery-autonomic-trends.md |
| **HRV stability** | Rolling CV of RMSSD over 14 days | Daily | "More variable than normal" — higher CV = less stable recovery |
| **Morphology stability** | Rolling IQR of window `qrs_median` over 30 days | Every 3 days | QRS width changes are slow; large shifts may indicate strap repositioning, not cardiac change |
| **T-wave stability** | Rolling TWA median over 30 days | Every 3 days | T-wave alternans trend; rising TWA tracked as "repolarization stability shifting" |
| **QT-RR coupling trend** | Linear slope of window `qt_rr_slope` over 30 days | Every 3 days | Flatter or steeper QT-to-RR adaptation vs personal norm |
| **Ectopic trend** | Weekly total ectopic fraction vs 90-day baseline | Weekly | "More early beats than usual this week" |

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 2. Trend Cards > 2.2 Trend card tier
content:
Each trend produces a tier assignment:

| Tier | Condition | User language pattern |
|---|---|---|
| `stable` | No significant slope (|trend_slope| < SE × 1.5) | "Your [metric] has been steady this week." |
| `shifting` | Significant slope within 1× baseline SD | "Your [metric] is trending [up/down]." |
| `notable_shift` | Significant slope and magnitude > 1× baseline SD | "Your [metric] has shifted noticeably this week." |
| `needs_more_data` | Insufficient windows for trend computation | "Still learning your pattern." |

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 3. Notable Patterns (formerly "Gentle Check-In Flags")
content:
Following `statistical-analyses/gentle-anomaly-check-in-flags.md`, but with a critical reframing: these are **"notable patterns,"** not "flags" or "alerts." The difference is real — a flag suggests something to worry about. A notable pattern says "here's something different, worth being aware of, but not inherently good or bad."

Every notable pattern uses observational language ("your heart rate was above your usual range") rather than diagnostic language ("your heart rate is abnormal"). The user is never warned or alarmed — they are informed and invited to reflect.

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 3. Notable Patterns (formerly "Gentle Check-In Flags") > 3.1 Algorithm
content:
```text
single_metric = robust_z(metric) > 2.0
multimodal = at least 2 of 6 core signals outside usual range
repeated = multimodal on 2 of last 3 valid days
extreme = any single robust_z > 3.5
pattern_found = repeated OR extreme
confidence_gated = pattern_found AND total_valid_hours_today > 12 AND data_quality_ok
```

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 3. Notable Patterns (formerly "Gentle Check-In Flags") > 3.2 Core signals
content:
| Signal | Observation direction | Why it is tracked |
|---|---|---|
| Overnight HR mean | Above or below baseline | Resting HR shifts with fitness, illness, stress, sleep, recovery [S11, S12] |
| RMSSD | Below or above baseline | HRV changes reflect autonomic balance; both low HRV (strain) and high HRV (rebound) are notable [S13, S14] |
| DC (deceleration capacity) | Below or above baseline | Vagal tone marker; low DC = reduced parasympathetic activity; high DC = strong vagal rebound — both are notable [PMC2886688, PMC12304026] |
| TWA (T-wave alternans) | Above baseline | Rising T-wave alternans indicates increased repolarization variability; tracked longitudinally per ISHNE-HRS ambulatory ECG consensus |
| EDR rate | Above or below baseline | Breathing rate changes with strain and recovery |
| Ectopic fraction | Above baseline | Increase in PVC/PAC frequency beyond personal norm |

**Important**: signals can be outside range in either direction. Low HR with high HRV after an active day is a recovery pattern, not a warning. Low HRV with high HR after poor sleep is strain. The pattern is notable either way — the framing changes from "your body is strained" (bad) to "your body is responding to yesterday" (neutral, informative).

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 3. Notable Patterns (formerly "Gentle Check-In Flags") > 3.3 Pattern significance tiers
content:
| Level | Rule | User language |
|---|---|---|
| `noticed` | 1 metric outside p10/p90 | "Your heart rate was a little outside your usual range overnight." |
| `interesting` | 2+ metrics outside p10/p90 OR 1 outside p5/p95 | "Several signals were different from your usual pattern last night." |
| `recurring` | Interesting pattern on 2 of 3 nights | "This pattern has appeared for a few nights now." |
| `check_in` | Recurring OR extreme | "Worth noting: several signals have been outside your usual range for [N] nights. Consider how you're feeling and whether anything has changed." |

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 3. Notable Patterns (formerly "Gentle Check-In Flags") > 3.4 Hysteresis
content:
- **Trigger**: require stronger threshold to surface than to remain visible (e.g., surface at `interesting`, remain visible at `noticed`)
- **Episode bundling**: if the same signal cluster was already surfaced within 72 hours, do not re-surface; update the existing episode silently
- **Clearing**: pattern clears after 2 consecutive valid days with all metrics within usual range
- **Cooldown**: after the user dismisses or acknowledges the pattern, suppress the same type for 7 days

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 3. Notable Patterns (formerly "Gentle Check-In Flags") > 3.5 Explainability template
content:
Every surfaced pattern has four components:

1. **What was different**: "Your resting heart rate was above your usual range, and your HRV was below your 60-day baseline last night."
2. **Compared to what**: "Your prior 60 nights in similar rest windows."
3. **How confident**: "High confidence: 7h 40m of good signal."
4. **What it might mean (optional)**: "This pattern often appears after physically demanding days, poor sleep, or when your body is fighting something. On your last 3 days with this pattern, you tagged 'heavy workout,' 'poor sleep,' and no tag." — grounded in the user's own history, not speculation.

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 3. Notable Patterns (formerly "Gentle Check-In Flags") > 3.6 Positive patterns (also surfaced)
content:
Not every notable pattern is about strain. When the heart shows adaptation — faster recovery, stronger vagal tone, new cardiovascular benchmarks — these are surfaced too, with celebratory or informative framing:

| Positive pattern | Detection | Framing |
|---|---|---|
| `recovery_improving` | Recovery speed (time to return to baseline) decreased by > 20% over 28-day trend | "Your heart is returning to resting rhythm faster after activity — a sign of improving cardiovascular fitness over the past month." |
| `hrv_trending_up` | 28-day HRV slope significantly positive | "Your overnight HRV has been trending upward. This can reflect improved recovery, better sleep, or fitness gains." |
| `rhr_trending_down` | 28-day RHR slope significantly negative | "Your resting heart rate has been drifting lower. This is a common sign of improving cardiovascular fitness." |
| `sleep_settling_faster` | HR drop rate at sleep onset increased by > 20% over 28 days | "Your heart is settling into rest more quickly at bedtime — a sign of better sleep onset quality." |
| `new_hr_benchmark` | Any window HR peak is a new personal best for that context class in 90+ days | "You reached [X] bpm — your highest sustained heart rate this season for [context description]. This suggests your cardiovascular capacity is expanding." |
| `new_hrv_benchmark` | Overnight RMSSD is a new personal best in 90+ days | "Last night's HRV was the highest you've recorded — a strong recovery signal." |

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 4. Adaptation and Recovery Tracking
content: Beyond individual patterns, the app tracks longer-term cardiovascular adaptation — how the user's heart is changing over weeks and months. This is where the longitudinal advantage shines: fitness, stress adaptation, and training response are invisible in a single ECG but emerge clearly in long-term trends.

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 4. Adaptation and Recovery Tracking > 4.1 Adaptation trend cards
content:
| Trend | Computation | Framing |
|---|---|---|
| **CV fitness proxy** | 60-day slope of resting HR ÷ weekly active minutes | "Your heart does more with less now — resting heart rate is dropping while you stay active." |
| **Recovery efficiency** | 60-day slope of recovery-to-baseline time after high-exertion windows | "You're bouncing back faster after exertion. Your body's recovery machinery is strengthening." |
| **Autonomic balance** | 60-day trend of DC + RMSSD in sleep windows | "Your parasympathetic activity during rest (your heart's 'recharge' phase) is strengthening." |
| **Rhythm consistency** | 60-day trend of sleep regularity index (SRI) | "Your rest rhythm is becoming more/less regular." |
| **Repolarization trend** | 60-day trend of QT-RR slope + TWA | "Your heart's electrical repolarization pattern is stable/shifting." |

heading_path: 04 — Longitudinal Analytics > 4. Adaptation and Recovery Tracking > 4.2 Milestones
content:
After 90+ days of recording, the app generates a milestone summary — not a daily check-in, but a retrospective:

> "**Your heart over the past 3 months**: your resting heart rate has dropped from 68 to 62 bpm. You've had 14 days where your HRV reached a new personal high. Your recovery after activity has gotten 22% faster. You've accumulated 180 context windows of data across 8 different activity patterns. Your heart is showing signs of cardiovascular adaptation."

This is the longitudinal payoff — the reason 24/7 wear matters. A single ECG at the doctor's office would never show these trends.

Per the engagement research (`clusters/engagement-explainability-trust.md`), explicit uncertainty language — "outside your usual range" — is safer and more useful than verdict language like "you are stressed" or "you are getting sick."

heading_path: Threshold: sleep_score > 0.65 for > 20 consecutive minutes
content:
Sleep is detected from the heart alone (no EEG, no wrist actigraphy required). The chest-strap ECG can derive HR, HRV, and respiration — cardiorespiratory patterns that shift predictably during sleep.

**Approach**: A dual-signal classifier operating on context windows:

| Signal | Awake pattern | Sleep pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Motion centroid | > 30 mG (typical) | < 30 mG sustained (body stillness) |
| HR mean | Variable | Dropping to resting minimum |
| RMSSD | Moderate | Elevated (vagal dominance) |
| DC (deceleration capacity) | Moderate | Elevated (parasympathetic dominance) |
| HR-to-RMSSD ratio | > 2.0 | < 1.5 (high vagal, low sympathetic) |
| EDR rate | Variable, 12-20 bpm | Slower, 10-16 bpm, more regular |
| HR stability | Variable | More stable within 30-min windows |

**Algorithm** (simplified, adapted from Frontiers Neuroscience 2026 cardiorespiratory sleep staging and MDPI Sensors 23/5/2390 CNN sleep-from-IBI research):

1. Identify candidate sleep windows: consecutive windows where `motion_centroid < 30 mG` for > 10 minutes
2. For each candidate, compute a sleep likelihood score:

```python
sleep_score = (
    w1 * (1 - sigmoid(hr_mean, midpoint=baseline_resting_hr, steepness=5)) +
    w2 * sigmoid(rmssd, midpoint=baseline_rmssd, steepness=0.05) +
    w3 * sigmoid(dc, midpoint=baseline_dc, steepness=0.1) +
    w4 * (1 - edr_variability_normalized) +
    w5 * (1 - hr_stability_inverted)
)

```

3. **Sleep onset**: first epoch where sleep_score crosses the threshold and stays above
4. **Wake time**: first epoch after the longest sleep block where motion > 50 mG AND HR rises > 10 bpm above nocturnal minimum
5. **Sleep duration**: total minutes between onset and wake time with sleep_score > 0.65

**Accuracy expectation**: 66-80% epoch-by-epoch agreement with PSG for four-class sleep staging from HRV alone, per research (MDPI Sensors 23/5/2390, Frontiers Neuroscience 2022). This is sufficient for sleep timing, duration, and regularity metrics — the use case this app targets. Fine-grained stage classification (N1/N2/N3/REM) is NOT attempted.

**Minimum data**: 14 valid sleep windows needed before sleep analytics report to the user.

heading_path: Threshold: sleep_score > 0.65 for > 20 consecutive minutes > 4.2 Sleep metrics
content:
Following `statistical-analyses/sleep-circadian-regularity.md`:

| Metric | Computation | Product translation |
|---|---|---|
| Sleep onset time | Clock time of sleep_score threshold crossing | "When your heart began settling for rest" |
| Wake time | Clock time of arousal criteria | "When your heart shifted to waking" |
| Sleep duration | Total minutes of sustained sleep_score > 0.65 | "Estimated resting heart hours" |
| Sleep midpoint | Midpoint between onset and wake | "Center of your rest rhythm" |
| Social jetlag proxy | Weekend sleep midpoint minus weekday sleep midpoint | "Weekend-weekday rest shift" |
| Sleep timing variability | SD of sleep onset over 7 days | "Schedule consistency" |

heading_path: Threshold: sleep_score > 0.65 for > 20 consecutive minutes > 4.3 Sleep Regularity Index (SRI)
content:
Adapted from GGIR documentation [S28] and `sleep-circadian-regularity.md`:

```text
For each pair of adjacent days:
    Compare sleep/wake state at each 30-minute clock-matching epoch
    SRI = agreement fraction across all pairs, scaled to [-100, 100]

where 100 = perfectly regular sleep schedule
      0 = random sleep pattern
```

SRI is computed over trailing 7 and 28 days. It is a rest-activity regularity metric — the name "Sleep Regularity Index" is retained for familiarity, but the app language should say "rest rhythm regularity" to avoid overclaiming sleep detection precision.

heading_path: Threshold: sleep_score > 0.65 for > 20 consecutive minutes > 4.4 Circadian HR metrics
content:
Following the nonparametric circadian metrics from `sleep-circadian-regularity.md` [S29]:

| Metric | Meaning | Product translation |
|---|---|---|
| 24h HR mean | MESOR (rhythm-adjusted mean) | "Overall heart activity level" |
| 24h HR amplitude | Peak-to-trough HR range over 24 h | "Day-night heart contrast" |
| Day-night HR difference | Mean HR in M10 (most active 10 h) minus mean HR in L5 (least active 5 h) | "How much your heart slows at night" |
| Acrophase | Clock time of peak HR in the fitted 24 h cosine | "When your heart tends to peak" (usually late afternoon) |

These are computed over 7-day windows using a basic cosinor model on hourly HR medians:

```text
hr(t) = mesor + amplitude * cos(2*pi*(t - acrophase) / 24)
```

Fitted via least squares. Only valid hours with > 30 min of good-SQI data are included.

heading_path: Threshold: sleep_score > 0.65 for > 20 consecutive minutes > 5. Recovery and Return-to-Baseline > 5.1 After-moment recovery tracking
content:
When a notable window is flagged (high exertion, ectopic cluster, notable HR surge), the app tracks how many windows (or hours, or sleep cycles) it takes for key metrics to return to within 1× MAD of the personal baseline:

| Metric | Recovery threshold | Tracked after moment type |
|---|---|---|
| HR mean | Return to within `baseline_median ± 1× MAD` | HR surge, high exertion windows |
| RMSSD | Return to within `baseline_median ± 1× MAD` | High exertion, poor sleep |
| Ectopic fraction | Return to < baseline p90 | Ectopic cluster |
| DC | Return to within `baseline_p10` (recovery of vagal tone) | Any notable moment |

heading_path: Threshold: sleep_score > 0.65 for > 20 consecutive minutes > 5. Recovery and Return-to-Baseline > 5.2 Response-to-context patterns
content:
Once enough data exists (60+ days, 20+ examples of a context transition), compute lagged associations:

```text
"If window type A (e.g., high-motion afternoon) is followed by window type B (e.g., low-motion evening):
    HR_mean in B tends to be X bpm higher/lower than baseline for B"
```

These are surfaced as pattern discoveries, not causal claims:

> "On days with high-activity windows in the afternoon, your overnight resting heart rate tends to be slightly above your baseline. This pattern has appeared in 14 of your last 20 high-activity days."

heading_path: Threshold: sleep_score > 0.65 for > 20 consecutive minutes > 6. Weekly Narrative
content:
Every 7 days, the app generates a narrative summary that answers three questions:

1. **What changed?** — Metrics whose 7-day trend deviates from their 28-day baseline
2. **What stayed stable?** — Metrics within normal range despite daily variation
3. **What might be worth trying?** — Gentle suggestions linked to observed patterns

Example:

> "**What changed**: Your overnight heart rate has been trending slightly above your 28-day baseline this week, and your HRV is a bit lower than usual. This pattern was present on 4 of 7 nights.
>
> **What stayed stable**: Your rest rhythm has been consistent — sleep onset within 30 minutes of your usual time on 6 of 7 nights. Your QRS and QTc intervals remain steady.
>
> **What to try**: If you've had unusual stress, less sleep, or more activity than normal this week, consider an easier day or two. Your heart tends to return to baseline within 2 days of rest days."

heading_path: Threshold: sleep_score > 0.65 for > 20 consecutive minutes > 7. Baseline Refresh and Drift
content:
Baselines are not static. A user who starts running will see resting HR drop. The baseline must adapt without chasing anomalies:

- **Slow adaptation**: EWMA with `alpha = 0.05` ensures it takes ~20 data points for a sustained change to shift the baseline by ~1/3 of the change magnitude.
- **Segment baseline on detected change**: If a trend persists for > 28 days in the same direction with a slope significantly different from zero, split the baseline into "before" and "after" segments. Surface this as: "Your baseline has shifted. Comparing to your new pattern since [date]."
- **Device/strap repositioning**: If morphology intervals (QRS width, R amplitude) show a sharp step change (> 3× MAD of prior 30 days in a single day), this is likely a strap repositioning, not a physiological change. The morphology baseline is reset. The HR/HRV baseline is unaffected.

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > Overview
content:
This document defines the information architecture the heart analysis feeds into — what the user sees, when, and at what depth. UI specifics (visual design, layout, Rive animations) are deferred; this is about the content, labels, narrative structure, and progressive disclosure layers.

The user's primary engagement with the app travels through these surfaces, from top to bottom in depth:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CW["Current Window Panel (glanceable)"] --> TL["Context Timeline (today)"]
    TL -.->|"tap a window"| WD["Window Detail Card"]
    TL -.->|"scroll to top"| DS["Daily Summary"]
    TL -.->|"weekly cycle"| WN["Weekly Narrative"]
    CW -.->|"notable pattern found"| CP["Check-In Prompt"]
    CF --> TE["Tag + Reflection"]
    WD -.->|"heart rhythm detail"| MI["Moment Inspector"]
    EV -.->|"tap a beat"| WF["Waveform Viewer (deepest)"]
    WD --> TR["Trend Cards (7d / 28d / 60d)"]
```

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 1. Current Window Panel > 1.1 What it shows
content:
The top of the main screen, always visible. Shows how the heart is behaving **right now** in the current context window.

| Field | Source | Update | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| Window context descriptor | `02-context-and-timeline.md` context vector | Each window boundary + on pull-to-refresh | "You've been still for 42 minutes" / "Moving steadily for the last 12 minutes" |
| Current heart rate | `hr_median` of trailing 10 beats (30 s rolling) | Every beat | "72 bpm" |
| Heart rate trend arrow | `hr_trend_slope` over last 60 s | Every 10 s | ↑ (rising > 2 bpm/min), ↓ (falling), → (stable) |
| HR vs baseline | `robust_z` of current window's partial `hr_mean` vs context-class baseline | Per beat (debounced to 5 s) | "Within your usual range" / "A bit above usual" |
| Signal quality indicator | `sqi` of current 1 s window | Every 1 s | Green dot (good) / Yellow dot (fair) / Gray (poor/absent) |

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 1. Current Window Panel > 1.2 Design principles
content:
- **Glanceable**: the panel should communicate at a glance whether everything is normal. An all-green panel = nothing needs attention. A shift in the baseline comparison line = something to look at.
- **Context-aware, not judgmental**: never "your heart rate is high" — always "above your usual range for times when you've been still." The context descriptor anchors the number.
- **Subtle animation**: the HR number pulses with each detected R-peak (like a heartbeat). This is a Rive opportunity. Rate of pulse = detected HR. Users should notice if the pulse animation stops (disconnected) or feels irregular (ectopy).
- **Respect silence**: if SQI = poor, the panel fades or shows a placeholder ("Adjust your strap — no good signal right now") rather than showing a garbage number.

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 1. Current Window Panel > 1.3 Language table
content:
| Situation | Context descriptor example | HR vs baseline line |
|---|---|---|
| Still, resting HR | "Quiet for 23 minutes" | "Resting heart rate: 62 bpm — in your usual range" |
| Still, elevated HR | "Still for 8 minutes" | "Heart rate: 84 bpm — a bit above your usual range for quiet moments" |
| Walking | "Moving steadily for 15 minutes" | "Heart rate: 98 bpm — typical for this kind of movement" |
| Exercising | "Active for 25 minutes" | "Heart rate: 142 bpm — in your active range" |
| Just stopped moving | "Settling down for 3 minutes" | "Heart rate: 88 bpm — recovering from activity" |
| Sleeping (detected) | "Resting overnight" | "Overnight heart rate: 54 bpm — in your sleep range" |
| Disconnected | "Strap not detected" | "No signal since 14:32" |
| Poor signal | "Checking signal..." | "Can't get a good reading — adjust your strap?" |

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 2. Context Timeline > 2.1 What it is
content: The day presented as an ordered stack of context window cards. This is the core UX — it makes the user's heart behavior across the day scannable and explorable. The timeline answers: "How did my heart spend the day?"

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 2. Context Timeline > 2.2 Timeline card content
content:
Each window card shows a compressed summary. The primary label is the **composite window score** (0-100, see `02-context-and-timeline.md` §"Composite window score"), not a word like "Quiet" or "Active" — words collapse gradients and feel judgmental; a number preserves the continuum.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 14:20 – 14:35  │  12/100  │  ○ 68 bpm mean     │
│   15 minutes   │          │  Heart settled      │
│                │          │  HRV: usual         │
│                │          │  No notable moments │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 14:36 – 14:58  │  68/100  │  ● 104 bpm mean    │
│   22 minutes   │          │  Active range       │
│                │          │  HRV: typical        │
│                │          │  2 PVCs detected    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Each card has:
- **Time bar** (start-end, duration)
- **Composite score** (0-100, the primary label) — derived from the window's continuous descriptor vector per `02-context-and-timeline.md`. The score is always **decomposable**: tapping it opens the score detail view showing the exact sensor values that produced it (motion centroid, motion variability, intermittency, phone motion, posture stability, heart-zone shift, SQI fraction). No opaque composite.
- **Heart behavior summary**: mean HR, a one-line description, HRV vs baseline, notable moment count (if any)
- **Tap to expand** → full Window Detail Card

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 2. Context Timeline > 2.3 Visual encoding
content:
- **Window height**: proportional to duration (longer = taller, within min/max bounds). A full sleep window would be the tallest block.
- **Score color**: three-point gradient (cool → warm) mapped from the composite score — low scores are cool blue-gray, mid are warm amber, high are warm orange. This creates a heat-map-like scannability: a day with lots of low scores is a rest day; a day with lots of high scores was active. The gradient derives from the score, which derives from the descriptor vector — never from a hard label.
- **Moment markers**: small dots or icons on cards with notable moments. PVC clusters get a "brief early beat" icon. Adaptation moments get a unique marker. Tapping the marker jumps to the Moment Inspector.

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 2. Context Timeline > 2.4 Timeline interactions
content:
- **Scroll**: vertical scroll through the day. Today is at the top; past days are below with date headers.
- **Day header**: "Wednesday, August 6" + summary line ("9 windows — mostly active morning, quiet afternoon, 7h 52m overnight rest")
- **Window tap**: expands to Window Detail Card (see §3)
- **Score tap**: opens the score detail view — the raw sensor descriptors that produced the composite score (`02-context-and-timeline.md` "Composite window score")
- **Long press**: "What were you doing? [Add context]" — optional tagging
- **Pull to refresh**: re-scans for new windows since last view

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 3. Window Detail Card
content:
Expanded view when a timeline card is tapped.

| Section | Content |
|---|---|
| **Context** | "Quiet, late afternoon, weekday" — descriptors from the window's `context` vector, written in natural language |
| **Heart rate** | Mean, median, range (p10–p90), min, max, trend direction, HR sparkline (small chart of HR over the window) |
| **Heart rhythm** | Beat type breakdown (normal/ectopic fraction), "2 early beats detected," "steady rhythm" or "occasional variation" |
| **HRV** | RMSSD, SDNN, DC, AC — with baseline comparison arrows |
| **Morphology** (if available) | PR, QRS, QTc medians — with "typical for you" or "slightly wider than usual" |
| **Breathing** | "Breathing rate: 14/min — regular" |
| **Notable moments** | List of detected moments within the window, each tappable for detail |
| **Signal quality** | "Good signal for 94% of this window" |
| **"Add a tag"** | Optional context: "I was... [working / relaxing / exercising / socializing / stressed / traveling / not sure]" |

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 4. Daily Summary > 4.1 Content
content:
| Section | Content |
|---|---|
| **Sleep block** | "7h 52m of resting heart rhythm. Your heart settled to 51 bpm overnight." + sleep metrics (onset, wake, regularity score) |
| **Day in windows** | "15 context windows. Mostly quiet morning, active mid-day, quiet evening." |
| **Heart journey** | "Your heart rate ranged from 51 bpm (sleep) to 143 bpm (active window at 16:12)." |
| **Notable moments** | 0-3 detected moments: "A brief cluster of early beats around 10:30 AM" / "Your heart rebounded strongly after the active window — HRV and resting rate both outside usual range" / "You reached a new peak heart rate for this kind of activity: 148 bpm" |
| **Compared to your baseline** | "Your resting windows were a bit above your 28-day average today. Your active windows were typical." |
| **Day confidence** | "Good signal for 18h 12m. 1h 48m of gaps." — always present to calibrate user trust |

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 4. Daily Summary > 4.2 Language patterns
content:
- Positive framing: "Your heart had a steady day" not "No problems detected"
- Pattern framing: "This is your third active day in a row — your overnight heart rate was slightly above baseline, which your body has done before after active stretches."
- Gaps as normal: "Your strap was disconnected for about 2 hours at lunch. That's fine — happens to everyone. We've shown what we could capture."

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 5. Weekly Narrative > 5.1 Three-part structure
content:
Per `engagement-explainability-trust.md`: "Weekly narrative summaries: What changed? What stayed stable? What might be worth trying?"

| Part | Content |
|---|---|
| **What changed** | Trends that moved outside baseline this week: "Your overnight heart rate trended slightly above your 28-day baseline on 4 of 7 nights." |
| **What stayed stable** | Metrics that held steady: "Your rest rhythm was consistent — sleep onset within 30 minutes of usual on 6 nights. QRS and QTc intervals remain steady." |
| **What might be worth trying** | Gentle, evidence-linked suggestions: "On your two rest days this week, your HRV recovered into your normal range. If your schedule allows, consider an easier day after active stretches." |

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 5. Weekly Narrative > 5.2 Pattern discoveries
content:
After 60+ days and 20+ context-transition examples:

> "**A pattern we've noticed**: After afternoon active windows (like your Tuesday bike ride), your overnight heart rate tends to stay 3-5 bpm above baseline. This has happened on 12 of your last 15 active days. On rest days, it settles back to your usual sleep rate."

These are framed as hypotheses, not facts — the user is invited to confirm or refine them.

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 6. Check-In Prompts > 6.1 What the user sees
content:
A subtle in-app banner (not a push notification — patterns are not emergencies):

> **"Several signals are outside your usual range today."**
>
> Your overnight heart rate was higher than usual, and your HRV is below your 60-day baseline. This pattern has shown up for 2 of the last 3 nights.
>
> This is not a diagnosis. It's a pattern worth noticing — it could be a demanding week, less sleep, or your body responding to something.
>
> **[How are you feeling?]**   **[I'll keep an eye on it]**

When the pattern is positive (e.g., recovery rebound, new HRV peak, faster recovery), the banner adapts:

> **"Your heart showed a strong recovery response last night."**
>
> Your overnight HRV reached a new high for this season (82 ms), and your resting heart rate settled unusually low. This is a sign your body is adapting well.
>
> **[Tell me more]**   **[Great!]**

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 6. Check-In Prompts > 6.2 Response options
content:
| User action | System response |
|---|---|
| Tap "How are you feeling?" | Opens a lightweight tag form: "I'm feeling... [fine / a bit off / not great / stressed / sick / recovering / poorly slept / big day / don't know]". The tag is attached to the pattern episode for future correlation. |
| Tap "I'll keep an eye on it" | Pattern is marked seen. Suppressed for 7 days for the same signal cluster. |
| No action | The pattern stays in the app but does not push-notify again for 72 hours (episode bundling). |

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 6. Check-In Prompts > 6.3 Language guardrails
content:
Explicitly avoid:

- "You may be getting sick" → "Several signals are outside your usual range — this can happen for many reasons"
- "Your heart is stressed" → "Your heart is working a bit harder than usual at rest"
- "Abnormal" anywhere → "Outside your usual range" or "A different pattern"
- "Alert" or "Warning" → "Pattern" or "Check-in"
- "Cardiac event" → "Notable moment"

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 6. Check-In Prompts > 6.4 Why not push notifications
content:
For consumer wellness, physiological deviations should not generate push notifications. Patterns are surfaced as in-app contextual content — part of the daily summary or timeline. The app is a tool for engagement and self-knowledge, not a monitoring sentinel. The user opens the app when they want to explore their heart; the app does not reach out to them.

The one exception: if the user has opted into a specific notification (e.g., "Tell me when my overnight pattern has shifted"), a single daily summary notification may fire. Even then, the language is neutral and observational.

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 7. Moment Inspector
content:
Tapped from a window detail card or moment marker on the timeline.

Shows a temporal view around the notable moment:
- A short ECG strip (~10 s, from the raw SBEC chunk) centered on the moment
- R-peak markers, beat type annotations
- A descriptive narrative: "5 PVCs in a 17-beat segment. Your heart returned to a steady rhythm afterward." or "After the active window, your heart rate settled to 48 bpm — below your usual range — and your HRV rose to 82 ms. This is a recovery rebound, a sign of good cardiovascular adaptation."
- Context tag: what the moment means in context — "This is your highest HR this season for windows where you've been moving steadily"
- Tappable individual beats → leads to Waveform Viewer

The Moment Inspector always answers three questions:
1. **What happened?** — the observation
2. **What does it mean?** — grounded in the user's own baseline, not medical interpretation
3. **Is this new?** — compared to the user's 90-day history

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 7. Moment Inspector > 7.1 Moment type framing
content:
| Moment category | What the inspector shows | Tone |
|---|---|---|
| Effort / achievement | "Reached 148 bpm — your highest sustained rate this season for moving-steadily windows. 12 bpm above your average for this kind of activity." | Celebratory, informative |
| Rhythm / pattern | "A brief cluster of 5 early beats over 17 heartbeats. This is a pattern your heart shows occasionally — you've had 3 similar moments in the past month, all during quiet windows." | Neutral, contextualizing |
| Adaptation / recovery | "Your heart rate settled 15 bpm below your usual resting range after activity, and HRV reached a personal high. This pattern — a strong recovery rebound — is a sign your body is adapting well to exertion." | Positive, educational |

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 8. Waveform Viewer (deepest layer) > 8.1 Content
content:
- ECG-paper-style scrolling view (like Heart Monitor 24 and clinical ECG viewers)
- PQRST delineation overlay (dotted lines marking Q-onset, R-peak, S-offset, T-offset; P-wave markers when present)
- Beat type annotations
- RR intervals between beats
- Pinch-to-zoom and horizontal scroll
- Tappable segments to see interval values

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 8. Waveform Viewer (deepest layer) > 8.2 Progressive disclosure
content:
The waveform viewer is **not the main screen**. It is deliberately deep — three taps from the main timeline (timeline → window detail → moment inspector → waveform viewer). This follows the progressive disclosure pattern validated by WHOOP and Heart Monitor 24 designs: "glanceable summary → metric detail → raw signal."

The waveform viewer is the place where engaged users (the 15% who want to "correlate specific metrics with lifestyle changes," per the WHOOP design breakdown) can explore. Most users will never open it, and that is correct.

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 9. Progressive Disclosure Summary
content:
| Layer | Content | Reach | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Current Window Panel** | HR, context, vs-baseline, SQI | Every app open | Top of screen, always visible |
| **2. Context Timeline** | Day as window cards | Every app open | Main scroll view |
| **3. Window Detail Card** | Full heart metrics for one window | When curious | Tap any window card |
| **4. Daily Summary** | End-of-day synthesis | Once per day | Top of timeline in the morning |
| **5. Check-In Prompt** | Notable pattern surfaced for reflection | When pattern triggers (infrequent) | Inline banner in timeline |
| **6. Weekly Narrative** | 7-day reflection | Once per week | Timeline top on the 7th day |
| **7. Moment Inspector** | ECG strip around a notable moment | When investigating a moment | Tap moment marker → detail |
| **8. Waveform Viewer** | Raw ECG with full delineation | Power users | Three taps deep from timeline |

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > 10. Things Intentionally Not Included
content:
- **Daily single-score (WHOOP-style Recovery)**: the project's own research warns against opaque composite scores. Individual metric cards with baseline comparisons are preferred — the user learns what matters to their body rather than trusting a black box. **Exception — the timeline composite score**: each window card carries a numerical score (0-100) for scannability, but it is explicitly *not* an opaque health verdict. It is decomposable by design — tapping it reveals the exact sensor values that produced it (`02-context-and-timeline.md` "Composite window score"). The distinction is transparency: if a score cannot be drilled into raw data, it does not ship.
- **Red/yellow/green traffic-light labels**: per `personal-baselines-anomaly-detection.md`, "usual range" / "slightly outside" / "well outside" is safer and more informative than color-coded verdicts.
- **Social comparison**: "Your HRV is higher than 73% of users" — the project strongly advocates within-person baselines over population norms. Social comparison is opt-in only, if ever.
- **Gamification (streaks, points, leaderboards)**: the app is for self-understanding, not competition. Streaks create anxiety when broken. Optional goal tracking ("3 active windows this week") may be useful later, but is not in scope now.
- **"Stressed" / "Recovered" / "Ready" labels**: the longitudinal research consistently warns against deterministic labels from wearable data alone. Descriptive statements ("HRV below your usual range") empower the user to interpret their own state.

heading_path: 06 — Engagement Surface > References
content:
- `../legacy/research/001-longitudinal-physiological-analysis/clusters/engagement-explainability-trust.md` (engagement analyses, confidence labels, user agency, narrative summaries)
- `../legacy/research/001-longitudinal-physiological-analysis/clusters/personal-baselines-anomaly-detection.md` (usual-range visualization, explainability, delay-diagnosis language)

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > Overview
content:
This document defines how the app persists raw ECG and derived data, how that data is uploaded for dataset building, and how test datasets are assembled for the offline analysis tooling. It supersedes the "raw data stays local only" posture from the design principles for this **research phase** — we persist everything so that data collection and dataset-driven testing are easy. The privacy posture is revisited before any public release (see the [decisions log](README.md#decisions-log)).

**Storage backend:** the **Longitud Supabase project** (`https://chfgywspomctrymxuxvf.supabase.co`) with Google OAuth, user-scoped RLS, private **`ecg-data`** Files bucket, and Postgres tables `profiles`, `recordings`, `ecg_chunks`, `context_windows`, `notable_moments`, `daily_summaries`. Schema reference: [`../supabase/migrations/001_longitud_schema.sql`](../supabase/migrations/001_longitud_schema.sql). The legacy SmashBeat sandbox project remains historical reference only ([`../SmashBeat-migration-sql/`](../SmashBeat-migration-sql/), [`../legacy/sandbox-migration-handoff.md`](../legacy/sandbox-migration-handoff.md)).

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 1. What Is Persisted > 1.1 On-device layout
content:
Everything under `filesDir/sandbox/<recording_id>/`, matching the Sandbox format ([`../legacy/sandbox-migration-handoff.md`](../legacy/sandbox-migration-handoff.md) §4):

```
filesDir/sandbox/<SBX-recordingId>/
  chunk_00000.bin          # SBEC raw ECG, 60 s
  chunk_00000_beats.jsonl  # per-beat records (schema v3 + morphology)
  chunk_00001.bin
  chunk_00001_beats.jsonl
  ...
```

| Artifact | Format | Content | Retained |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raw ECG chunk | SBEC v1 (`01-signal-pipeline.md` §7) | int32 µV samples at 130 Hz | Yes — needed for waveform viewer, reprocessing, and offline re-delineation |
| Beats JSONL | schema v3 extended (`01-signal-pipeline.md` §6) | per-R-peak RR/HR/RMSSD, context features, morphology | Yes — needed for window metrics and re-analysis |
| Window/timeline | on-device SQLite | `PerWindowMetrics`, day summaries, baselines | Yes — lightweight summaries |
| Supabase metadata | Postgres (`recordings`, `ecg_chunks`, `context_windows`, `notable_moments`, `daily_summaries`) | recording span, per-chunk storage paths, window `metrics_json` (morphology), checksums, upload state | Yes |

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 1. What Is Persisted > 1.2 Upload units
content:
- The **chunk** (60 s) is the atomic upload unit, matching the Sandbox cadence (§4.7: 60 s chunks, 15 s rotate check, 15 s upload kick, 4 chunks/batch, 24 batches/cycle).
- Raw ECG is never uploaded in memory buffers; it is always chunked, written, zstd-compressed, then uploaded.

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 2. Upload to Supabase > 2.1 Target layout
content:
| Object | Location |
|---|---|
| Raw ECG chunk | `ecg-data/{user_id}/{recording_id}/chunk_{index:05}.bin.zst` |
| Beats JSONL | `ecg-data/{user_id}/{recording_id}/chunk_{index:05}_beats.jsonl.zst` |
| Recording row | `recordings` (id `SBX-<epochMillis>`, `user_id`, device_id, started_at, ended_at, status) |
| Chunk row | `ecg_chunks` (recording_id, chunk_index, storage paths, beat_count, byte_size, checksum, compression, uploaded_at) |
| Context window | `context_windows` (`window_id`, `context_class` — composite key since 2026-08-19, `tags_json` jsonb, `metrics_json` jsonb — full morphology + HRV + PRSA) |
| Notable moment | `notable_moments` |
| Daily summary | `daily_summaries` (per `user_id` + date) |

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 2. Upload to Supabase > 2.2 Upload behavior
content:
| Concern | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Compression | zstd level 3 via `SandboxCompression`; graceful fallback to uncompressed (`compression = "none"`) |
| Idempotency | `x-upsert: true` on storage; metadata upsert via `Prefer: resolution=merge-duplicates`; local SQLite state machine `pending → uploaded / missing_local` prevents double-upload |
| Offline handling | chunks stay `pending` locally; WorkManager periodic job (`NetworkType.CONNECTED`) + in-process drain loop retry on reconnect |
| Post-sign-in backfill | `LocalDataBackfillRepository` runs on Google sign-in and on cold start with a restored session: upsert all local `sandbox_recordings`, drain pending chunks, then sync unsynced analytics (`context_windows`, `notable_moments`, `daily_summaries`) |
| Ongoing upload toggle | **Auto-upload** in Session tools gates `SandboxUploadScheduler.kick` during recording; backfill is always attempted when authenticated |
| Network conservatism | uploads only on a connected network (`NetworkType.CONNECTED`); Wi-Fi-only toggle deferred to public release (see §5) |
| Checksum | SHA-256 of the uncompressed `.bin` stored in `sandbox_chunks.checksum` — used by the dataset tooling to verify integrity after download |

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 2. Upload to Supabase > 2.3 Auth and RLS
content:
The app gates on **Google OAuth** (`AuthGate` + supabase-kt ComposeAuth). Uploads use the authenticated session JWT (not anon-only). RLS on all tables: `user_id = auth.uid()`. Storage policies scope paths to `{user_id}/…` on the private `ecg-data` bucket — created in [`../supabase/migrations/003_storage_bucket_policies.sql`](../supabase/migrations/003_storage_bucket_policies.sql) (insert/update/select/delete for `storage.objects` under the caller's own user-id folder). Configure `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`, and `GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID` in `longitudinal-app/secrets.properties` (see `secrets.properties.example`).

> **Gotcha:** the chunk-upload RLS failure (`403 new row violates row-level security policy` in the Session tools Upload Queue panel) is caused by missing `storage.objects` policies for the `ecg-data` bucket. `001` only documented a suggested policy in a comment; `003` actually grants the authenticated user CRUD over their own `{user_id}/…` folder. Without it, storage object inserts are denied while the `ecg_chunks`/`recordings` metadata tables still accept rows.

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 3. Dataset Tooling (Outside the App)
content:
The dataset build tooling is **separate from the mobile app**, lives on Windows, and is not part of the app repository's runtime. Contract:

| Capability | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Pull recordings from Supabase | `run_qa.py export` — authenticated Storage GET on `ecg-data/{user_id}/…` via the **service-role key** (bypasses RLS for bulk research pulls; `DATASET_BACKEND=longitud` selects the current schema/bucket) |
| Verify integrity | decompress zstd, recompute SHA-256, compare to `ecg_chunks.checksum` |
| Reconstruct recordings | reassemble contiguous chunks into full-recording SBEC + beats JSONL |
| Re-delineate offline | re-run R-peak detection + PQRST delineation on the raw ECG (using the more robust Dart reference segmenter approach from [`../legacy/sandbox-migration-handoff.md`](../legacy/sandbox-migration-handoff.md) §4.3) |
| Build labeled test datasets | assemble subsets (per subject, per context condition, per quality tier) for the Phase-C test harness (`08-testing-and-development-phases.md`) |
| Inventory users/recordings | `list_users.py` — service-role read of `profiles`/`recordings` before any pull |
| Re-analyze to composite context | `analysis/analyze_users.py` — batch `_recording_windows` over exports; per-user composite `context_class` + tags + moments + daily summaries |
| Upgrade stored legacy rows | `upgrade_context_windows.py` — legacy 3-bin `context_class` → composite key + tags (dry-run / `--write`) |

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 3. Dataset Tooling (Outside the App) > 3.1 Backend selection
content:
`dataset-tooling/sandbox/config.py` reads `DATASET_BACKEND`:

- **`sandbox`** (default, unchanged): legacy SmashBeat project — `sandbox_recordings` / `sandbox_chunks`, bucket `sandbox-ecg`, `subject_id` key. Existing exports and `reimport_top_chunks.py` are untouched.
- **`longitud`**: current app project — `recordings` / `ecg_chunks` / `context_windows`, bucket `ecg-data`, `user_id` key. Requires `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` (see `.env.example`); the anon key reads nothing because of per-user RLS.

Both backends write the same standard export layout, so downstream tooling (`run_qa.py verify/inventory/report`, `run_tests.py`, `analyze_users.py`) is backend-agnostic:

```
data/exports/<timestamp>/
  <recording_id>/
    recording.json
    chunks.csv
    chunks/chunk_XXXXX.bin
    chunks/chunk_XXXXX_beats.jsonl
```

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 3. Dataset Tooling (Outside the App) > 3.2 User-data analysis flow
content:
```mermaid flowchart LR SB[Supabase Longitud] -->|"service-role key"| LU[list_users.py] SB -->|"service-role key"| EX[run_qa.py export --all-users] EX --> DIRS["data/exports/<ts>/<recording_id>/"] DIRS --> AU[analysis/analyze_users.py] AU --> R["results/analyze/<user_id>/
<recording_id>.json + rollup"] SB -->|"service-role key"| UP[upgrade_context_windows.py] UP --> UPR["results/upgrade_<ts>.json (dry-run) or
upserted context_class + tags_json"] R -->|"--check-against"| UP ``` - `analyze_users.py` drives the shared `tests._recording_windows` engine over every exported recording (skips and reports any without `chunks.csv`) and writes a per-recording summary shaped like the T15 real pass, a per-window `*_windows.jsonl` detail file, and a per-user `rollup.json` (window count, class population, tags, moments, daily summaries). - `upgrade_context_windows.py` pages all stored `context_windows`, and per user runs one causal `StreamingBaseline` pass: `time_of_day`/`day_type` from `start_ms` (UTC wall-clock by default, `--tz` overrides), `rhythm` from `global_quantile("hr", …)` read before the window updates the baseline, `motion` from `motion_centroid_mg` + the `is_sleeping` heuristic, and `tags` from `metrics_json` vs the class p20/p80 — exactly the `_recording_windows` classification loop. The metric lookup tolerates the app's camelCase `metrics_json` keys (`hrMedian`, `rmssdMs`, `dcMs`, `edrRate`) alongside the offline snake_case shape. Rows whose `context_class` already contains `-` are skipped. Default is a **dry-run report**; `--write` upserts `context_class` + `tags_json` (migration [`002_add_context_window_tags.sql`](../supabase/migrations/002_add_context_window_tags.sql)). - `--check-against results/analyze` cross-checks the upgraded keys/tags against the re-analyzed windows on overlapping recordings: matching is by largest **interval overlap** (the app persists 60 s on-device windows while the offline engine segments the same raw data on its own ~11 min grid), and it reports per-axis disagreement (`time_of_day` / `day_type` / `rhythm` / `motion`) plus samples.

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 3. Dataset Tooling (Outside the App) > 3.2 User-data analysis flow
content:
**Executed 2026-08-19** on the Longitud project: `--all-users` export found 1 user / 18 recordings, of which only 3 had uploaded chunks (114 chunks, ~2 MB; the rest are zero-chunk sessions). Re-analyzing those 3 produced 22 composite windows (18 good, 7 populated classes, tags + moments). All 605 legacy `context_windows` rows were converted and upserted in place — verified 0 rows remain with 3-bin keys and 321 rows carry non-empty `tags_json` (sleeping-only windows legitimately have none). Cross-check on the overlapping overnight session shows `time_of_day`/`day_type` always agree; `rhythm`/`motion` diverge because the upgrade streams all 605 stored windows per user (60 s app grid, per-user resting-HR) while re-analysis streams each recording's beats on the offline grid — expected scope difference, recorded in the report's note. T15 passes unmodified on the exported Longitud recording (`results/t15_longitud_export.json`), and the unit suite (122 tests incl. the camelCase-metrics regression) is green.

The tooling consumes the same chunk schema and storage layout defined in §1–2, so the app and tooling can evolve independently as long as the chunk contract stays stable.

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 4. Privacy Posture
content:
| Phase | Posture |
|---|---|
| Research/development (now) | User-scoped Supabase with Google sign-in; morphology in `context_windows.metrics_json`; legacy SmashBeat data stays in the old project |
| Public release (later) | Revisit: consent copy, data deletion UX, offline-first default |

This decision is recorded in the decisions log with its revisit trigger.

heading_path: 07 — Persistent Storage and Test Datasets > 5. Resolved Decisions (Phase-A Build)
content:
- **Network conservatism**: uploads run on any connected network (`NetworkType.CONNECTED`), batch = 4 chunks, up to 24 batches per cycle. No Wi-Fi-only toggle in Phase A — research collection favors maximum data throughput. A Wi-Fi-only / mobile-data-threshold setting is added before public release.
- **Subject model**: replaced free-text `subject_id` with **`auth.users.id`** as the storage partition key. `SubjectIdDialog` removed; account shown in Session tools.
- **Retention**: local chunk files kept on device after upload (re-upload / debug); cloud sync requires sign-in. Offline USB export removed — Supabase is the export path.
