heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > Overview
content:
This project is **built from the results of testing datasets**. We first build what is needed for data collection, then build tests that analyze the datasets to find the best implementations. The approach in the spec documents is a starting point; measured outcomes on real H10 data drive changes, and every change is recorded in the [decisions log](README.md#decisions-log).

```
Phase A ──► Phase B ──► Phase C ──► Phase D
collect       tooling      test       full app
```

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 1. Phase A — Light Data-Collection App
content:
Build the minimum app needed to gather longitudinal H10 data. This is **not** the full product; it is a capture instrument.

| Capability | Source of truth |
|---|---|
| Polar H10 BLE streaming (130 Hz ECG, 200 Hz ACC) | [`01-signal-pipeline.md`](01-signal-pipeline.md) §1; [`../legacy/sandbox-migration-handoff.md`](../legacy/sandbox-migration-handoff.md) §3 |
| SBEC + beats JSONL v3 chunks (60 s) | [`07-storage-and-datasets.md`](07-storage-and-datasets.md) §1; handoff §4.1–4.2 |
| zstd compression + Supabase upload (chunk queue, WorkManager) | [`07-storage-and-datasets.md`](07-storage-and-datasets.md) §2; handoff §3.3, §4.5–4.7 |
| Basic recording UI (subject, H10 pick, start/stop, status) | handoff §2.3 (channel contract), §2.4 (manifest) |
| SQI tagging on-stream | [`01-signal-pipeline.md`](01-signal-pipeline.md) §2 |

**Out of scope for Phase A**: full PQRST delineation, context segmentation, window metrics, longitudinal analytics, engagement surfaces. The app persists raw chunks and beats JSONL (with SQI); everything analytical happens offline in Phase B/C.

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 2. Phase B — Windows Analysis Tooling
content:
Separate tooling, **not in the app folder** (see [`07-storage-and-datasets.md`](07-storage-and-datasets.md) §3). Runs on Windows, consumes the dataset contract.

| Module | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Dataset importer | pull recordings from Supabase, verify checksums, reassemble chunks |
| Offline delineation | re-run R-peak detection + PQRST delineation on raw SBEC (reference: handoff §4.3 Dart segmenter) |
| Metric computation | compute window metrics, HRV, morphology intervals from beats JSONL |
| Ground-truth helpers | annotate datasets (e.g., manually reviewed beats, synthetic ECG, reference detector output) |
| Visualization | ECG strips, delineation overlays, interval scatter plots, segmentation boundaries |

Phase B is where P-wave detection consistency is measured (see §4.2).

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 3. Phase C — Offline Test Harness
content: A reproducible harness that runs a prioritized test matrix against collected datasets. Each test reports pass/fail against provisional criteria; results update the decisions log and spec thresholds.

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 3. Phase C — Offline Test Harness > 3.1 Test matrix
content:
| # | Test | What it validates | Revisit trigger it feeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | R-peak detection vs reference | Sensitivity/PPV of the Pan-Tompkins variant against a reference detector on good-SQI windows | `README.md` decisions log: delineation accuracy |
| T2 | P-wave detection consistency | Detection rate + fiducial stability of P-onset/P-offset across good-SQI windows; sensitivity to strap orientation, amplitude, HR | Proposal 3 — see §4.2 |
| T3 | TWA MMA at 130 Hz | Modified Moving Average (MMA) at native 130 Hz (vs clinical 500 Hz reference) — noise rejection, threshold stability | decisions log: TWA entry |
| T4 | QT-RR slope stability | Slope stability within short windows; sensitivity to window length and ectopy | decisions log: QT-RR entry |
| T5 | Window segmentation boundary precision | Change-point detection vs hand-labeled context transitions; merge/split behavior; HR-fused dual-channel boundaries (motion ∪ heart) since 2026-08-19 | `02-context-and-timeline.md` parameters |
| T6 | Beat classification (PAC sensitivity) | PAC/PVC detection sensitivity + precision vs ground truth | decisions log: beat classification entry |

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 3. Phase C — Offline Test Harness > 3.1 Test matrix
content:
> **Implemented 2026-08-13** — `dataset-tooling/analysis/beat_classify.py` runs the §1 rules against each beat's raw SBEC morphology + on-device features. Synthetic injected-PAC/PVC/escape suite: 100% sensitivity on all classes. Real-data pass on `SBX-1786604523753` (295 usable chunks, 18,133 beats): 80.6% normal, 0.51% ectopic (86 PAC / 6 PVC / 2 escape), 1.6% artifact, 17.3% unknown. `peak_confidence` was dropped from the artifact rule and template seeding (diluted metric, same reasoning as the 2026-08-12 on-device gate change); chunk-edge beats fall back to rhythm-only classification. See decisions log 2026-08-13.
>
> **T6 follow-up 2026-08-13** — the 17.3% unknown share was characterized: ~40% were session-template staleness (beat matches a locally-built template but not the stale session template) and ~60% were genuinely wider-QRS morphology in the morning/vehicle hours (not phone GPS — 0/34,653 beats; not strap motion — flat across ACC buckets). The classifier now (a) re-seeds the template on sustained drift (rolling median corr of the last 50 regular beats < 0.85 → rebuild from the most recent 30 segments), (b) keeps a secondary-morphology template of the most recent 20 failing beats and accepts beats matching it as normal, and (c) uses a 1.8× (was 1.4×) QRS width ratio bound to absorb the 130 Hz estimator's ±2-sample jitter. Re-run: **unknown 17.3% → 6.0%**, normal 80.6% → 92.1%, ectopic 0.36%, artifact 1.56%; synthetic suite still 100% sensitivity on all classes; 2 new unit tests (drift re-seed, secondary morphology) green. See decisions log 2026-08-13.
>
> **Implemented 2026-08-13** — `dataset-tooling/analysis/quality_gate.py` + `run_t7` implements T7 (gap / quality handling) against the `03-heart-metrics-and-events.md` §5 window gates and `01-signal-pipeline.md` §1.2 gap timeline. Synthetic suite: all 6 window-gate cases fire exactly per spec (ok / sparse / degraded / high_ectopic_period / gap_compromised, incl. gap-over-degraded precedence) and gap detection finds an injected 10-min gap with no false positives on a dense stream (8 unit tests). Real-data pass on `SBX-1786604523753` (34,653 beats, 9.5 h): coverage **0.9999** (one 3.6 s stream-startup gap, matching the known chunk-0 loss), 114 five-minute windows → **77 ok / 37 degraded** (0 sparse, 0 gap_compromised, 2 high_ectopic_period). Degraded windows concentrate in the last ~6 h with quiet ACC (mean 5–15 mg) — signal/contact wear, not motion; the 2 ectopic-flagged windows coincide with elevated ACC (26 / 83 mg, commute). The on-device `signal_quality = poor` label (2,207 beats, 6.4%) is only 56% explained by independent motion / RR / contact signals — the gate is broader than the spec's §2.1 SQI components. See decisions log 2026-08-13.
>
> **Sample-offset compensation 2026-08-13** — a fixed-shift attempt at compensating the on-device `sample_offset` group delay (8-17 samples after the raw QRS deflection, calibrated on `micahz` + `micahhh-pre-fix`) *raised* unknowns to 24% (template smearing, delay varies beat-to-beat). Replaced with per-beat re-delineation: `_qrs_peak` scans [`sample_offset - 30`, `sample_offset + 5`] for the max positive deflection 3-20 samples before the on-device peak and centers all morphology/width/trust windows on it. This exposed a width-estimator bug: the onset scan stopped at half-amplitude one sample from a sharp R sample (→ ~15 ms, `None`), and the S-wave recovery logic produced spurious 31 ms / 108-131 ms widths for beats that are the template morphology. Rewrote the estimator to a baseline-crossing onset + J-point offset (return within a 15% amplitude band after the S-wave trough), collapsing the width histogram to the 46-54 ms band. T6 re-run on `SBX-1786604523753`: **unknown 4.54% → 0.32%** (59 beats), normal 93.6% → 97.8%, ectopic 0.34%, artifact 1.56%; synthetic suite still 100% on all classes. Width-guard validation: guard now recovers 1 unknown and keeps 16 premature beats from being misread as PVC (untrusted ramp width not used for the wide verdict). Pre-fix recording `SBX-1786580067052__reprocessed` re-run: unknown 1.0%, ectopic 2.3%. All 28 unit tests green. See decisions log 2026-08-13.
>
> **Classifier stress matrix 2026-08-13** — with only two raw datasets available (the 2026-08-12 exports are metadata-only), coverage is broadened synthetically: `dataset-tooling/stress_classifier.py` runs the T6 rules across 16 scenarios the app will meet in the wild (HR range, amplitude range, inverted polarity, baseline wander, noise, wide-QRS dominant rhythm with a narrow PAC, big-T, PVC coupling sweep, secondary morphology, poor-SQI), each in a true-position pass and a device-delayed pass that exercises `_qrs_peak`. All scenarios hold **100% sensitivity on all classes in both passes**; NaN/flat/huge inputs never crash (4 new unit tests, 32 total). One documented spec edge case: at slow HR (RR 1200 ms) an escape at 2160 ms trips the >2000 ms artifact ceiling before the escape rule — kept as-is (matches the on-device reference gate). See decisions log 2026-08-13.
>
> **T5 gate 2026-08-13** — the real-data pass on `SBX-1786604523753` produced 2,485 windows (median 7 s) purely from coverage fragmentation: `segment_with_gaps` treated every beatless second as a gap, and all 2,491 beatless seconds on this session are ≤ 5 s beat-misses (zero real gaps). `segment_with_gaps` now linearly interpolates NaN runs ≤ 5 s (`MAX_INTERP_GAP_S`; real gaps still split), which collapses the session to **68 windows (median ~4 min, min 62 s)**. Boundary validation via candidate-review: `plot_segmentation.py` renders 13 per-45-min PNGs (1 s ACC RMS + HR + activity bands, detected boundaries shaded, ACC/HR/label change-point candidates dashed) and emits a `t5_labels.json` starter; `compare_segmentation.py` matches confirmed labels to nearest detected boundary. Provisional self-labeling (candidates agreeing with a boundary within 30 s + strong ACC changes ≥ 25 mG): **median boundary error 8.5 s (criterion ≤ 10 s), 84.2% within 30 s**; 31 strong change-points (mostly commute-hour ACC bursts) have no boundary and 29 boundaries have no independent ACC/HR change-point support — those boundaries coincide with HR-only transitions at low ACC (HR jumps 60→80+ bpm while ACC stays 5–15 mG), which the ACC-only change-point detector cannot see but the adaptive MAD threshold does. Outcome: **algorithm kept** (gap interpolation fix retained; no parameter change); final confirmation of the label set is the user's candidate-review pass over the PNGs. See decisions log 2026-08-13.
>
> **T5 candidate auto-validation + gate closure 2026-08-15** — the manual 174-row candidate review never happened (too many rows on noisy timelines), so `dataset-tooling/analysis/candidate_validate.py` + `validate_candidates.py` replace it with an offline, look-ahead validator. Every candidate and every detected boundary is judged on ACC and HR independently: valid iff settled level shift ≥ `NOISE_FACTOR` (2.0) × **local-noise MAD** (45 s just before the edge — the full pre-window MAD is inflated by the previous activity burst, which had rejected real transitions like t=228), the new level **holds** ≥ `MIN_HOLD_S` (60 s) with ≤ `GAP_TOL_S` (10 s) dips tolerated (real bursts dip), and (ACC only) the change is edge-concentrated ≥ `EDGE_FRACTION` (0.2) so a gradual ramp is not a sharp transition (HR is exempt — heart rate changes physiologically gradually, so a sustained HR step is valid regardless of sharpness, per the user decision that HR-only sustained transitions are valid context windows). Windows tuned to the algorithm's local scale: pre 90 s / post 120 s / guard 30 s. **Verdicts on micahz (`SBX-1786604523753`)**: **61/67 detected boundaries valid (91%)** — the 6 invalid ones are genuinely flat (ACC ≤ 1 mG, HR ≤ 1 bpm shifts, e.g. t=21532 ACC 3.6→3.8) and are the plausible false splits; **36/55 deduped candidates valid (65%)**; false-split rate **9%**, missed rate **19%** (7/36 validated candidates with no boundary within 120 s — HR-only and burst transitions the ACC-only algorithm cannot see). Boundary error via `compare_segmentation.py` on candidate-only validated labels: overall median **15 s** / p90 65 s / 62% within 30 s — inflated by a burst-pairing artifact (a burst yields two boundaries start+end but one candidate peak, so the greedy matcher force-pairs them, e.g. burst-end boundary t=31805 vs burst-start candidate 31727); on same-transition matches (≤ 30 s) the median error is **6 s** (p90 18 s), inside the ≤ 10 s criterion. **Outcome: algorithm kept**; `segment_with_gaps` stays ACC-only under test and the HR-fusion question is logged for `02`. Verdict PNGs (green=valid / red=invalid) in `data/results/t5_plots/` for spot-review. See decisions log 2026-08-15.
>
> **T5 HR fusion implemented 2026-08-19 (self-calibrating context model plan)** — `segmentation.py` gains a second segmentation channel: a 1 Hz HR epoch series (`epochs_from_beats_hr`, per-second median of beat HR from good/fair-SQI beats, `60 000 / rr_ms`) built from the same beats as the motion epochs. The adaptive-threshold change-point detector runs on both channels with identical parameters and the **union** of committed boundaries is re-windowed before the merge-short + fluctuation-guard post-processing (ACC-only behavior is a strict subset, so the validated motion-boundary precision holds). The context model itself is replaced by a **self-calibrating composite class** (`{time_of_day}-{day_type}-{rhythm}-{motion}`, `04` §1.2): 8 time-of-day bins, weekday/weekend, a 5-bin `rhythm` axis whose quintiles (p20/p40/p60/p80) come from the user's own global HR t-digest (causal — read before the window updates the baseline; population prior 75 ± 15 bpm on cold start), and a 3-bin motion axis (sleeping/sedentary/active, fixed 20 mG threshold). Optional per-window tags (`is_waking`, `recovery`, `elevated`, `challenge_window`) ride alongside but never enter the baseline key. See decisions log 2026-08-19.
>
> **Implemented 2026-08-13** — `dataset-tooling/analysis/window_metrics.py` + `run_t8` implements T8 (per-context-window heart metrics) against `03` §2/§4/§5: HR summary (harmonic-mean + median + p10/p90 + min/max + trend slope + stability), time-domain HRV + Poincaré + PRSA DC/AC (ectopic + post-ectopic RR exclusion; ≥30 / ≥120-beat minimums), RSA + amplitude EDR with agreement quality, morphology medians (QRS / R-amp / QT / QTc Bazett + Fridericia / PR / QT-RR slope), rhythm counts with `all_beats` denominators, and the §5 quality gates. Synthetic pass (7 cases) asserts hand-computed HR/RMSSD/SDNN/pNN50/DC/AC/ectopic-exclusion values. Real pass on `SBX-1786604523753` (570 chunks, 34,646 beats, **68 windows median 236 s**): **43 ok / 20 degraded / 5 sparse**; metric coverage HR 1.0, HRV 0.93 (short windows), PRSA DC 0.63 (needs ≥120 beats), EDR/morphology/TWA ≥0.98; window summary hr median 59.7 bpm, RMSSD 58.2 ms, DC 5.1 ms. The 43/20/5 split is consistent with T7's 77/37 on 5-min buckets (T7 has no sparse bucket because 5-min windows always have beats; context windows can be 62 s). See decisions log 2026-08-13.
>
> **Implemented 2026-08-13** — `dataset-tooling/analysis/moments.py` + `run_t9` implements T9 (notable-moment detection) against `03` §3: all §3.1–3.3 rules behind a pluggable `Baseline` (per-context-class percentiles; rhythm/pattern rules baseline-free), notability tiers §3.5, output schema §3.4. Synthetic pass (11 cases): clean baseline fires nothing; every injected pattern (hr_peak, hr_deep_rest, ectopic_cluster, bigeminy, trigeminy, pause absolute+relative, surge, drop, hrv_peak, dc_peak, edr_low, twa_notable, vagal_rebound, hr_sustained_new_peak) fires. Exploratory real pass on `micahz` with a **within-session self-baseline** (provisional; production needs 90 days of context-conditioned data): 254 moments / 68 windows — 110 effort/achievement, 144 rhythm/pattern, 0 adaptation/recovery. Beat-level rules run **only on good/fair-SQI beats** (spec §2 inclusion rule) — without the filter the degraded late-session signal yielded 217 ectopic_cluster, with it 75; the residual share reflects the T6 relative-prematurity rule labeling rate-transition runs (RR 1200→820 ms in chunk 217) as ectopic and needs hand-labeled rhythm to resolve. twa_notable (35) uses the 15 s MMA max (200–735 µV on isolated high-HR/noise bins) while window twa_median stays <10 µV, so it is only `noticed` pending multi-day trend confirmation. See decisions log 2026-08-13.
>
> **Cross-session validation 2026-08-13** — `SBX-1786500028785` (pre-fix detector, 15.57 h, 934 chunks) was reprocessed with the fixed detector (`reprocess_beats.py`; 63,874 beats vs 143,843 device-recorded — the pre-fix ~2.25× over-detection, same finding as `micahhh`). Reprocessed beats omit H10 ACC (motion lives only in the original stream), so `patch_reprocessed_acc.py` copies ACC/context from the originals by time-match. T6/T8/T9 re-run: **T6** unknown 0.52% / normal 93.6% / ectopic 4.22% / artifact 1.38% on 663 usable chunks (48,807 beats) — classifier stability holds cross-session on the unknown level (0.32% on micahz), but **ectopic is 4.2% here vs 0.34% on micahz**, matching the reprocessed-micahhh 2.3%: the T6 relative-prematurity rule labels rate-transition runs as ectopic systematically, not just on micahz. **T8** 112 windows (median 316 s): 110 ok / 0 degraded / 2 sparse (zero degraded is a reference-gate SQI property — no `poor` label; not a metric-stack difference); coverage HR 1.0 / HRV 0.94 / PRSA 0.63 / morphology 0.99, matching micahz. **T9** 633 moments — 213 ectopic_cluster (cross-session confirmation of the rate-transition labeling) and a **new 170 `hr_coupling_jump` cluster** (~1.5/window on a session with real motion: 38 active/high-motion windows vs micahz's mostly-still) — the rule is noise at `noticed` tier and needs a min-duration/consolidation review. 0 adaptation/recovery again (no challenge→next-window pairing). See decisions log 2026-08-13.
>
> **T6 follow-up 2026-08-14 (rate-adaptive rhythm reference)** — the 4.22% ectopic / 78-beat PAC runs on the cross-session recording traced to the spec's "mean RR over last 10 *normal* beats" reference: a beat flagged premature never enters the normal-RR history, so once a genuine rate change starts the reference stays at the old slow mean and every beat at the new rate is flagged the same way — a cascade, not ectopy. `beat_classify.py` now compares prematurity/escape against the **median of the last `RATE_REF_WINDOW` (10) non-artifact RRs** (`recent_rrs`, fed by every beat that passes the artifact gate; `normal_rrs`/`_mean_normal_rr` removed). The median adapts to a sustained rate change within a few beats while a single premature beat (one short RR among nine) does not move it; 0.80× / 1.50× fractions unchanged. 4 new unit tests (rate-step no-cascade, gradual-ramp no-cascade, genuine premature still flagged, genuine escape still flagged) — 12 T6 tests green. Re-run: **cross-session ectopic 4.22% → 1.35%** (48,807 beats; longest premature run 78 → 6 beats; 50 runs ≥3 beats all ≤6, the remainder genuine rate-change transients such as a 969 ms beat against a 1334 ms median) and **T9 `ectopic_cluster` 213 → 3**; **micahz ectopic 0.34% → 0.10%** (18,133 beats) and `ectopic_cluster` 75 → 15 (remaining are true clusters / pauses; `pause` 29 → 0 was the earlier good/fair-SQI inclusion filter, the rule is RR-only and unchanged). See decisions log 2026-08-14.
>
> **Hand-labeling of the 50 residual premature runs 2026-08-15 (T6 residual-ectopy validation)** — `dataset-tooling/label_ectopic_runs.py` rendered every post-fix premature run (≥3 consecutive pac/pvc beats, `SBX-1786500028785__reprocessed`, 50 runs / 202 beats) as a PNG with pre-run RRs + per-beat `local_premature` (rr < 0.80 × median of the preceding 3 beats) and embedded the labeling rubric. Audit found 4 concrete issues that were fixed: run 11 had a justification string written into boolean beat fields (restored `local_premature`/`chunk_edge`, moved observation to run-level `notes`, label `true_ectopy`); run 39's first beat is cropped at a chunk edge → relabeled `uncertain`; runs 17/32 had autocomplete-corrupted notes claiming "all local_parameter flags == false" (corrected to state the first 1-2 beats are locally premature with a smooth descent → transition). The `true_ectopy`-vs-`transition` ambiguity ("slow → fast → slow" vs "beat → pause → beats → pause → beat") was unresolved with only 1 pre + 1 post beat of context, so the tool gained **post-run RR context** (`post_rrs`, next 5 RRs after the last run beat), a **`post_pause` indicator** (`max(post_rrs) / median(pre_rrs)` — a compensatory pause reads ≫ 1, smooth return ≈ 1), **wider PNGs** (4 s pre / 4 s post vs 2 s / 1.5 s), and a **label-preserving `--refresh-context` mode** (re-extracts context by chunk+first-beat-index while keeping existing `label`/`notes`). **Re-review verdict (50/50 labeled): 26 transition / 12 true_ectopy / 7 detector_artifact / 5 uncertain**. Post-pause separates the labels: true_ectopy median `post_pause` 1.20 (range 1.00–1.40) vs transition 0.79 (0.60–1.36) and detector_artifact 0.91 (0.77–1.08). Under that rule, 3 former `true_ectopy` runs (15/20/44) with no post-run pause (smooth return to baseline, `post_pause` ≤ 1.09, first post-RR ≈ pre-baseline) were downgraded to `transition`, and 1 former `transition` run (28) with all five post-RRs above the pre-baseline (1477/1385/1431/1331/1400 vs ~1181) was upgraded to `true_ectopy` (compensatory-pause signature). **Verdict: T6's residual ectopic labeling is dominated by rate transitions (26/50 runs, 118 beats) and detector re-triggering (7 runs, 28 beats), not true ectopy** — beat-level precision (true_ectopy / all labeled beats) **0.188** (38/202), definite precision excluding `uncertain` **0.207** (38/184). The rate-adaptive reference left genuinely short runs (≤6 beats) that are mostly real rhythm changes; true ectopy exists but at the low expected rate for a healthy session. See decisions log 2026-08-15.

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 3. Phase C — Offline Test Harness > 3.1 Test matrix
content: > **T6 run-resolution pass 2026-08-15** — the labeling study left the residual premature runs (26 transition / 7 artifact / 12 ectopy) labeled by hand, so `dataset-tooling/analysis/premature_resolution.py` now automates that verdict as a **post-classification look-ahead pass** (wired into `_t6_real_pass` and `_recording_windows`, so both T6 counts and T8/T9 window metrics + `ectopic_cluster` moments see the resolved labels). Every consecutive `pac`/`pvc` run (all lengths, including singles) is judged from the rhythm on both sides: (1) **detector re-trigger** — any run beat ≤ 400 ms (`RETRIGGER_RR_MS`, the ~300 ms refractory floor; covers the labeled artifacts whose fast pre-rhythms broke an "all ≤ 0.62×pre" gate) with no pause → `artifact`; (2) **compensatory pause** — `max(first two valid post-run RRs) / median(pre-run RRs) ≥ 1.12` (`PAUSE_FRACTION`) → kept as `pac`/`pvc`; (3) else → `normal` (rate transition). Runs at the recording edges (no pre-run rhythm or < 2 valid post-run RRs) are left unchanged. Two calibrations came from the failing labels: the pause reads the **first two post-run beats**, not the five-beat max — transitions 9/12/26/49 had *late* or artifact-inflated slow RRs (e.g. run 12's post `[762, 846, 38, 1400, 1377]`), while every true-ectopy run shows the pause within the first two beats; and the artifact gate is a **refractory floor** rather than an all-beats-short fraction, which correctly catches artifacts on fast pre-rhythms (runs 2/3/5/6/25, pre-medians 462–577 ms) while leaving transition run 34 (662–762 ms) untouched. **Reproduces the 50 human labels 44/45 (97.8%)** — all 26 transitions → normal, all 12 true_ectopy kept, all 7 detector_artifact → artifact; the single residual mismatch, run 49 (transition labeled, first-two-post pause 1.15), sits inside the true_ectopy range (floor 1.14) and is irreducible by RR alone. **6 new unit tests** (transition→normal, ectopy kept, re-trigger→artifact, end-of-recording unchanged, single PAC with pause kept, single short RR without pause→normal). **Re-run both sessions**: cross-session `SBX-1786500028785__reprocessed` ectopic **1.35% → 0.45%**, premature runs 439 → 153 (max run 6 → 5), `ectopic_cluster` T9 moments **3 → 0**; micahz `SBX-1786604523753` ectopic **0.10% → 0.01%** (1 PAC), premature runs 14 → 1, `ectopic_cluster` **15 → 1**. Residual premature beats on cross-session: 221 (217 pac + 4 pvc); the kept micahz `ectopic_cluster` (1) still needs a morphology check. See decisions log 2026-08-15.

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 3. Phase C — Offline Test Harness > 3.1 Test matrix
content:
> **T9 follow-up 2026-08-15 (`hr_coupling_jump` consolidation)** — the cross-session false-positive cluster (170 moments vs 4 on micahz, ~1.5/window) was fixed in `analysis/moments.py`. The rule now runs as `_hr_coupling_jump` (replacing the inline per-beat-pair block): adjacent pairs with |ΔHR| ≥ 20 bpm and ≤ 60 s spacing are clustered into one HR-shift event when their start times fall within `COUPLING_CLUSTER_S` = 60 s, and **exactly one moment is emitted per event** (duration spans the cluster, `hr_delta` = max Δ, `motion_mg` = max sustained motion) instead of one per qualifying pair. Motion must now stay elevated ≥ `MOTION_SUSTAIN_BEATS` = 3 consecutive beats above the pre-jump baseline (`_sustained_motion_jumps`); a single-beat >3× spike no longer fires, and the ±30 s proximity window is kept as `MOTION_PROXIMITY_S`. **New coverage**: T9 synthetic case `hr_coupling_jump` (asserts exactly one moment on a two-step 60→86→115 bpm transition with sustained motion — the old rule emitted two) + 3 unit tests (one-per-transition, single-beat-spike no-fire, no-motion no-fire). **Re-run both sessions**: cross-session **170 → 43** (`hr_coupling_jump` moments; per-window 0.38, down from ~1.5), durations now 0.5–83 s (a real shift cluster vs the old 3–5 s single pairs), hr_delta 20–109; micahz **4 → 2** (per-window 0.03). The residual 43 on cross-session are distinct HR-shift-with-movement events on a session with 38 active/high-motion windows, not near-duplicates. See decisions log 2026-08-15.

> **Implemented 2026-08-15** — `dataset-tooling/analysis/baseline.py` (`StreamingBaseline`) + `run_t10` implements T10 (incremental baseline) against `04` §1.3/1.4: per-context-class streaming sufficient statistics (n, mean, M2, EWMA α=0.05, self-contained t-digest), empirical-Bayes (James–Stein) shrinkage of sparse classes toward a cross-context prior, Student-t (n−1 df) band widening, and confidence tiers **learning → establishing → established** replacing the hard minimum-windows gate. Drop-in compatible with `moments.Baseline` so `detect_window_moments` runs unchanged. Synthetic pass (4 cases): EB shrinkage reduces small-sample error (aggregated over 60 sparse classes), bands converge to the true p10/p90, tiers fire at n=5/14, early false-flag rate 0.209 vs nominal 0.20 (Student-t correction). Real passes (T8 window sets re-derived): **micahz** (`SBX-1786604523753`, 21 windows / 20 good, 3.6 h) time-to-first-reportable **2.83 h → 0.41 h (7×)**; **cross-session** (`SBX-1786500028785__reprocessed`, 112 windows / 110 good, 15.57 h) **1.78 h → 0.54 h (3.3×)**. Band width (HR, still class) converges 80–99 bpm at n=1 → ~18 bpm at n≥14; final streaming estimate tracks the session batch baseline within ~1 bpm (78.9 vs 78.0; 82.5 vs 82.0). Sparse classes (active n=4, high_motion n=8) get a usable tiered baseline instead of nothing. 7 new unit tests; full suite 78 green. See decisions log 2026-08-15.

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 3. Phase C — Offline Test Harness > 3.2 Provisional pass criteria (examples — to be tuned during Phase B)
content:
| Test | Provisional criterion |
|---|---|
| T2 P-wave | ≥ 90% detection rate on good-SQI resting windows with median adjacent-beat PR repeatability ≤ 15 ms (revised 2026-08-13: ≈2 samples @ 130 Hz is the wearable hardware floor; fiducials measured at 500 Hz) |
| T3 TWA | median TWA < 47 µV on clean resting windows with no drift over a session |
| T4 QT-RR | slope stable within ±20 ms/s across 5 min windows at similar HR |

These are starting thresholds, not contracts. Test outcomes can (and will) revise them.

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 3. Phase C — Offline Test Harness > 3.3 Outcome → decision flow
content:
```
For each test:
  run on collected dataset(s)
  └─► measure vs criterion
        ├─ pass        → keep spec; note coverage
        ├─ fail        → change the approach (algorithm, threshold, or suppress the feature);
        │                record in decisions log with date + evidence
        └─ inconclusive → define what dataset/labeling is needed; collect more
```

The full app (Phase D) is built only after the Phase-C tests establish which algorithms and thresholds work on real H10 data.

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 4. P-Wave Detection Consistency Test > 4.1 Motivation
content: P-waves are often visually small on H10 waveform viewers. Before the app relies on P-wave-derived metrics (PR interval, P duration, P amplitude), the Phase-C tooling must measure how consistently they can be detected on real H10 data.

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 4. P-Wave Detection Consistency Test > 4.2 What is measured
content:
| Measurement | Definition |
|---|---|
| Detection rate | Fraction of beats in good-SQI windows where a P-wave is found |
| Fiducial stability | Repeatability of P-onset/P-offset across consecutive similar beats |
| Orientation sensitivity | Detection rate split by strap position / module orientation (if available) |
| Amplitude distribution | P-wave amplitude histogram — how often it approaches the noise floor |
| HR sensitivity | Detection rate vs heart rate (faster HR compresses the search window) |

heading_path: 08 — Testing and Development Phases > 4. P-Wave Detection Consistency Test > 4.3 Decision gate
content:
> **Resolved 2026-08-13** — gate **closed: "show with caveat"** (downgrade/suppress not supported by the evidence).
>
> With P-wave fiducials measured on the 500 Hz cubic-spline-upsampled window (the §5.4 on-device path, added to `pwave.py`), the re-run on `micahz` (`SBX-1786604523753`, 295 good-SQI chunks, 18,047 beats) gives:
> - **Detection rate 0.9581** (criterion ≥ 0.90) — up from 0.9544 pre-upsample; P-amplitude median ~198 µV, only 1.8% < 30 µV.
> - **Adjacent-beat PR delta median 14.0 ms / p95 174 ms** — passes the revised ≤ 15 ms criterion.
>
> **Criterion change**: the provisional ±10 ms PR-repeatability criterion was below the hardware floor. At 130 Hz one sample is 7.7 ms, so automated PR error on a wearable patch is ~2 samples (~15 ms) even with good delineation (VitalPatch @ 125 Hz: arXiv:2108.00536; Springer 10.1007/s13239-022-00617-3). Fibion's sampling guide requires 250–500 Hz for P-wave/ST visibility, which the 500 Hz fiducial path now provides. Criterion is now **median adjacent-beat PR delta ≤ 15 ms** (p95 stays informational).
>
> **Policy**: P-waves are detectable and displayed; P-derived metrics (PR, P-dur, P-amp) are visually presented per `01` §5.5 but excluded from automated flags and from window-metric medians until the on-device 500 Hz path is implemented. The strap-orientation caveat stands (Polar H10 feasibility study: ResearchGate 363193345 — P-waves harder on 1-lead chest belt, but basic rhythm evaluation still matches 12-lead in 94–100%). See decisions log 2026-08-13.

heading_path: 09 — UI Kit, Layout, and Tabs (v0.1 cinematic instrument) > Design pillars
content:
1. **Warm white canvas, near-black ink.** Background `#FCFCFA`; primary text `#0A0A0A`. Gray ramp carries hierarchy (`#525252`, `#8A8A86`, `#D9D9D4`, `#ECECE8`, `#F4F4F1`).
2. **Flat instrument controls.** No Duolingo lip/rim button system. Primary = black fill + white text; Secondary = 1 px outline; Ghost = text only. Press = subtle fill lerp, not shadow travel.
3. **Panels are bordered, not elevated.** `InstrumentPanel` = white fill, 1 dp border, 16 dp radius; selected state = 1.5 dp ink border.
4. **One semantic accent.** Desaturated red `#C0392B` reserved for LIVE indicator dot and stop/end actions. Color means data meaning, not decoration (`06` §10).
5. **Type pairing.** Space Grotesk (display, body, CTAs) + IBM Plex Mono (every numeric readout, tech labels, `tnum`). Bundled in-app.
6. **No gradients, no shadows.** Depth = border weight, selected stroke, and segment texture on the timeline rail.
7. **No fake metrics.** Fields show `—` until the data path exists.

09 — UI Kit, Layout, and Tabs (v0.1 cinematic instrument) > Component library > `ContextTimelineChart`
content:
Replaces the flat `ContextTimeline` label row (which used `joinToString` and misaligned labels from proportional segments). **Layout:** legend row (`HR ↑` · `Motion ↓` · `— — No sensor` · `● Live`), proportional axis ticks at 0% / 50% / 100%, Canvas track with center baseline, **HR bars up** and **motion bars down** per segment, and a **per-segment label row** where each cell uses `Modifier.weight(segment.weight)` so labels stay under their track columns. **Zoom:** `OVERVIEW` (full 12 h) and `TIME OF DAY` (wall-clock bin slices, below). Token: `timelineHeight` 152 dp, `timelineTrack` 12 dp.

Continuous horizontal rail with time-proportional weighted segments. Each segment has a label, weight, optional `startMs`/`endMs`, `hrBpm`/`motionMg` for bar heights, and `TimelineSegmentState` (Default, Selected, Estimated, LowConfidence, NoData, Live). **Day axis:** `6A · 12P · 6P`; **night axis:** `6P · 12A · 6A`. Segments are **tappable** (hit-test by cumulative width) and drive `ContextInspectorBody`.

**Segment labels:** context windows show `{hr}·{motion}` (e.g. `72·18` = HR bpm · motion centroid mg); gaps with no sensor data show `no sensor` (dashed NoData texture). **Live overlay:** while recording, a trailing `Live` segment from `recordingStartedAtMs → now` shows live HR/motion, and its inspector carries the **live composite context label** (`{time_of_day}-{day_type}-{rhythm}-{motion}`, see zoom modes below) instead of a hardcoded "Live"; when connected but not recording and no windows yet, a single connected segment replaces full-period `no sensor`.

**Period model (Home):** 12 h blocks — **Day** 6:00–18:00, **Night** 18:00–6:00 (spans midnight). Header chips: `DAY` / `NIGHT` + `PREVIOUS` / `CURRENT` + `OVERVIEW` / `TIME OF DAY` / `LIVE`. Default kind follows local clock.

heading_path: 09 — UI Kit, Layout, and Tabs (v0.1 cinematic instrument) > Component library > `LiveWaveform` / `TrendGraph`
content: `LiveWaveform` draws the **zoomed, smooth-scrolling** live ECG. It consumes an atomic `EcgFrame` (`samples` + monotonic `counter`) from `SandboxRecordingService.ecgFrame()` so the ring snapshot and global index cannot race. Internally a `WaveformScroller` ring holds ~4 s of samples; the display **lags the live feed by ~1 s** (SmashBeat-style delayed feed) and advances with a `withFrameNanos`-driven scroll edge using a **fractional sample accumulator** (exactly `sampleRateHz` samples/s, no per-frame truncation drift). The visible slice is ~2.8 s of data (≈3–4 QRS complexes, auto-scaled to the slice min/max), with a vertical sweep line at the right edge. When no samples exist yet the canvas renders the `noData` texture. `TrendGraph` draws the RR/HR history from `rrHistory` (the rolling RR interval `StateFlow`). Annotations: `LIVE 2.8S`, `LAST 5 MIN`.

heading_path: Heart Analysis Approach for a Longitudinal ECG App > Overview
content:
This document set defines a complete, on-device heart analysis approach for a mobile app that conducts cardiovascular analysis from a Polar H10 chest strap worn 24/7. The analysis is designed for the common user — someone who wants to understand how their heart behaves day to day across different life contexts, not just when something goes wrong.

The approach is statistics-and-heuristics only. No machine learning is designed here; the ECGFounder foundation model is explicitly deferred to a future phase.

Core metrics are computed per beat and per context window: heart rate, time-domain and PRSA-based HRV (RMSSD, SDNN, deceleration capacity DC / acceleration capacity AC), EDR respiration, and PQRST morphology intervals. **PRSA-based deceleration capacity (DC) is the primary autonomic metric alongside RMSSD** — it is robust to noise and non-stationarity on 24/7 ambulatory data and is a validated marker of cardiovascular state (see `03-heart-metrics-and-events.md` and the decisions log).

**Every choice in these documents is a starting point, not a contract.** The agent building this out should adjust any metric, threshold, or design decision when new information, validation data, or better judgment surfaces, and record those changes in the decisions log below.

heading_path: Heart Analysis Approach for a Longitudinal ECG App > Design Principles
content:
| Principle | Translation into the app |
|---|---|
| **Within-person inference** | Every metric is reported relative to the user's own baseline, not a population norm. RHR, HRV, morphology intervals, and rhythm metrics vary substantially between people. |
| **Context-aware, not context-labeled** | Heart behavior is computed inside stable "context windows" segmented from raw motion data. There are no hard tags like "sedentary" or "running" — context is described by continuous descriptors (motion intensity, posture, time-of-day). |
| **Longitudinal rhythm, not single-moment snapshots** | The core UX is a context-segmented timeline. A day is an ordered list of context windows, each with a heart-behavior summary. |
| **Gentle flags, not diagnostic alarms** | Deviation from baseline triggers a check-in nudge ("Several signals look different from your usual range"), never a health verdict. Notable moments include positive events (new HRV peaks, faster recovery, vagal rebound) — the heart does interesting things, not just concerning things. |
| **On-device, privacy-preserving** | All beat detection, morphology delineation, context segmentation, window metrics, and daily aggregation happen on the phone. No cloud dependency for core analytics. **Research-phase exception**: during development we persist raw ECG to the SmashBeat sandbox Supabase project to build test datasets (see `07-storage-and-datasets.md`). This posture is revisited before any public release. |
| **Transparent uncertainty** | Every insight carries a confidence level tied to signal quality, wear time, and data completeness. Low-confidence summaries are softened or hidden. |
| **Progressive depth** | Glanceable current-window summary → context timeline → metric detail → raw waveform viewer. Depth is opt-in. |
| **Behavior-linkable, not prescriptive** | Patterns are framed as associations: "After high-activity windows, your overnight HRV tends to dip," not "You should train less." |

heading_path: Heart Analysis Approach for a Longitudinal ECG App > Pipeline
content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    H10["Polar H10: 130Hz ECG + 200Hz ACC"] --> AQ["Acquire + quality gate (SQI, gap bridging)"]
    Phone["Phone ACC / AR / GPS bursts"] --> CTX["Context descriptors (continuous, no tags)"]
    AQ --> BD["R-peak detection + PQRST delineation"]
    BD --> F1["Per-beat features (RR, HR, RMSSD, morphology intervals)"]
    CTX --> WS["Context-window segmentation (change-point + hysteresis)"]
    F1 --> WF["Per-window heart metrics (HR/HRV/DC-AC/EDR/notable moments)"]
    WS --> WF
    WF --> TL["Context-segmented timeline + daily summary"]
    TL --> LA["Longitudinal analytics: baselines, trends, gentle flags, sleep/circadian"]
    LA --> ES["Engagement surface: current panel, timeline, weekly narrative"]
    ES --> AM["Adaptation milestones (90-day retrospectives, CV fitness gains)"]
    F1 --> ST["Persistent storage (chunks + upload to sandbox Supabase)"]
    ST --> DS["Test datasets (Windows tooling pulls from Supabase)"]
    DS --> TH["Offline test harness (Phase C)"]
    TH -.->|"results revise thresholds/algorithms"| LA
    TH -.->|"results revise thresholds/algorithms"| WF
    TH -.->|"results revise thresholds/algorithms"| BD
```

Three pipelines run concurrently on the phone, plus a storage/upload path and an offline testing loop:

1. **Real-time pipeline** (per sample, ~100 ms cadence): FIFO buffer, R-peak detection, per-beat tagging (quality, premature/ectopic classification), per-beat morphology raw values. Output: beats JSONL (every detected R-peak with context snapshot), matching the SmashBeat Sandbox format.
2. **On-window-close pipeline** (when a context window boundary is confirmed, ~60 s min window): aggregates beats in the closed window into window-level metrics, computes HR/HRV/DCA/EDA summaries, detects events, and appends the window to the day timeline.
3. **Daily aggregation pipeline** (at the end of the main sleep window, or on app open after midnight): baseline updates, trend recalculation, notable pattern detection, weekly summary update. Triggers only when enough valid data exists.
4. **Storage/upload path**: raw chunks + beats JSONL persist on-device and upload to the sandbox Supabase project for dataset building (see `07-storage-and-datasets.md`).
5. **Offline testing loop**: datasets pulled from Supabase feed a Windows test harness whose results revise thresholds and algorithms (see `08-testing-and-development-phases.md`).

heading_path: Heart Analysis Approach for a Longitudinal ECG App > Key Hardware Constraints (Polar H10)
content:
| Constraint | Value | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| ECG sampling rate | 130 Hz (fixed) | ~7.7 ms resolution; upsample to ~500 Hz for interval precision beyond beat detection |
| Battery (streaming) | ~6 days continuous BLE streaming | Users must recharge/replace CR2025 every ~5-6 days; gaps are normal |
| H10 offline memory | ~20 h RR intervals only, no raw ECG | Gaps <20 h can recover HR/RR data but lose morphology and ACC; gaps >20 h are data-missing |
| BLE range | ~10 m | Phone must stay nearby; brief dropouts are expected |
| ACC streaming | 200 Hz, gravity-inclusive mG | Gravity-free dynamic RMS computed by subtracting 2 s moving average per axis |
| ECG packages | 73 samples per BLE packet (~0.56 s) | Timestamped at arrival; BLE jitter of tens of ms is acceptable for beat-level context |
| RR accuracy | Within 2 ms (validated across activities) | Superior to phone-based PPG; can use H10 RR as ground truth for beat timing |

Sources: Polar H10 white paper [polar.com], Polar BLE SDK issue #169 [github.com/polarofficial/polar-ble-sdk], MDPI validity studies [mdpi.com/1424-8220/26/3/855, mdpi.com/1424-8220/22/17/6536], JOEM feasibility study [ovid.com/joem].

heading_path: Heart Analysis Approach for a Longitudinal ECG App > Sources > Web resources
content:
- **Polar H10 spec/validity**: Polar H10 white paper, Polar BLE SDK docs, MDPI Sensors validation studies (HRV accuracy, ECG waveform quality, RR interval precision)
- **Delineation algorithms**: EPFL modular low-complexity delineator, wavelet-based 32-bit integer online delineation (PMC3076264), Prominence method vs DNN comparison (medrxiv 2026.03.24.26349185), Pan-Tompkins on ARM Cortex-M4
- **Single-lead event detection**: Huawei single-lead arrhythmia validation (PMC10475230), XGBoost beat classification on wearable ECG (PMC8398252), 1D U-Net for PAC/PVC detection on single-lead (MDPI Sensors 26/2/513)

- **Deceleration capacity**: PRSA-based DC as vagal marker (PMC12304026, PMC6932416), DC/AC sensitivity to aging (PMC2886688)
- **T-wave analysis**: T-wave alternans MMA method on Holter monitoring (PMC10222557, JAHA 10.1161/JAHA.123.033619), Tp-e as repolarization dispersion marker (MDPI PMC11221957)
- **ECG aging and morphological features**: ECG age from wearable single-lead with Extended-12 feature set (npj Digital Medicine 10.1038/s41746-026-02344-8), ambulatory ECG consensus on QT dynamics and ST shifts (ISHNE-HRS 2017 Heart Rhythm journal)
- **Engagement design**: WHOOP design breakdown (925studios.co), Fitbit adaptive cardio load (2025), "The More You Give the Wearable" (Springer 2025), "Look into your Heart" speculative visualization (arXiv 2511.07600v1), Heart Monitor 24 (Google Play)
- **Vagal rebound and recovery**: parasympathetic reactivation after exercise (Frontiers Physiology 10.3389/fphys.2025.1579929), cardiac autonomic recovery from submaximal exercise (IJERPH 10.3390/ijerph19169797), heritability of vagal rebound (Eur J Appl Physiol 10.1007/s00421-016-3459-y)

| 2026-08-06 | Context windows segmented by motion change-point detection, not by labeled activity | User explicitly rejects hard tags; continuous descriptors let users discover their own patterns; avoids misclassification harm | If window segmentation produces too many false boundaries or windows shorter than minimum duration |
| 2026-08-06 | Deceleration capacity (PRSA) as primary autonomic metric alongside RMSSD | PRSA is robust to noise and nonstationarities (key for 24/7 ambulatory data); DC is a validated mortality predictor and sensitive to aging; adds depth beyond standard HRV | If computational cost of PRSA per-window is prohibitive on mobile |
| 2026-08-06 | Sleep windows detected from HR/HRV patterns (no EEG/PSG claim) | ECG-derived sleep staging is feasible (66-80% accuracy vs PSG); chest-strap ECG can also derive respiration; avoids requiring a second device; sleep timing/regularity is what matters for engagement, not stage detail | If sleep onset/offset error is too large for useful circadian analytics in H10-only data |
| 2026-08-06 | Beat classification (normal/PVC/PAC) via rhythm-interval rules with morphology confirmation | On-device, no ML; validated in Huawei smartwatch single-lead algorithm (macro-F1 92.9% for 4-class); morphology template match adds specificity | If PAC sensitivity is too low without DNN (noted at 0.54-0.80 in literature) |

1. Problem Statement & Intent

1.1 Objective

Design and implement a real-time software pipeline capable of ingesting a live, raw ECG telemetry stream (specifically from a **Polar H10** sensor via Bluetooth LE at **130 Hz**) to dynamically segment individual heartbeats and continuously calculate clinical time-domain intervals (**PR interval, QRS duration, QT/ST segments**).

```
        ▲          R (Peak)
        │         / \
        │        /   \                 T (Peak)
Signal  │       /     \               / \
(mV)    │ P    /       \             /   \
        │/\   /         \___________/     \____
        ┼──\─/───────────\─────────/───────────►
        │   Q             S                   Time (ms)
        │
        │◄─PR─►◄──QRS───►◄───────QT───────────►
```

1.2 Core Technical Challenges

- **Streaming Constraints:** Processing must occur dynamically using a sliding window or rolling buffer, avoiding batch processing architectures.
- **Deterministic Latency:** The system must account for a physiological look-ahead window (the T-wave concludes up to 450ms _after_ the R-peak) while maintaining real-time performance.
- **Signal Corruption:** High susceptibility to motion artifacts, electromyographic (EMG) muscle noise, and baseline wander due to respiration in wearable environments.

---

2. Real-Time System Architecture

To prevent data loss from the Bluetooth LE thread, ingestion must be decoupled from digital signal processing (DSP) using a thread-safe, First-In, First-Out (FIFO) concurrent circular buffer.

```
┌───────────────────────┐      Push      ┌─────────────────────────┐
│  Polar H10 BLE Stream │───────────────►│ Thread-Safe FIFO Buffer │
│       (130 Hz)        │                │    (3-Second Capacity)  │
└───────────────────────┘                └─────────────────────────┘
                                                      │
                                                      │ Pull (Every ~100ms)
                                                      ▼
                                         ┌─────────────────────────┐
                                         │ Real-Time DSP Pipeline  │
                                         │  (Filtering & Splines)  │
                                         └─────────────────────────┘
                                                      │
                                                      ▼
                                         ┌─────────────────────────┐
                                         │   R-Peak Optimization   │
                                         │    (Pan-Tompkins/WT)    │
                                         └─────────────────────────┘
                                                      │
                                                      ▼
                                         ┌─────────────────────────┐
                                         │     Delineation Layer   │
                                         │ (Slope/Wavelet Engine)  │
                                         └─────────────────────────┘
                                                      │
                                                      ▼
                                         ┌─────────────────────────┐
                                         │ Physiological Validator │
                                         └─────────────────────────┘
```

2.1 The 3-Second Rolling Window Strategy

- **Buffer Size:** Maintain a fixed array of exactly **390 samples** (3 seconds × 130 Hz).
- **Execution Interval:** Trigger the downstream segmentation engine every time a new data packet arrives (typically 10–20 samples), or when a new R-peak is flagged.
- **The Look-Ahead Lag:** When an R-peak is identified at index t, the system pauses segmentation for that specific beat until t + 65 samples (500ms) have populated the buffer, ensuring the T-wave is fully captured.

---

3. Best Possible Algorithmic Approaches

Approach A: Rule-Based First & Second Derivative Delineation

_Highly optimized for battery-powered systems, mobile devices (Kotlin/Swift), and low-resource environments._

1. **Mathematical Transformation:** Compute the first derivative \(y'[n]\) and second derivative \(y''[n]\) using central finite differences to capture instantaneous velocity and acceleration of the voltage curve:  
    \(y^{\prime }[n]=\frac{x[n+1]-x[n-1]}{2}\)
2. **QRS Localization:** Identify the sharpest positive slope (\(y'[n] = \text{max}\)) and sharpest negative slope (\(y'[n] = \text{min}\)) within a localized zone around the R-peak. The **Q-onset** is marked where \(y'[n]\) crosses an adaptive near-zero threshold before the upward surge. The **S-offset (J-point)** is marked where the negative slope stabilizes back to the baseline.
3. **P & T Wave Windows:**
    - Search for the **T-wave** within a dynamic search window spanning \(R_{\text{peak}} + 100\text{ms}\) to \(R_{\text{peak}} + 450\text{ms}\).
    - Search for the **P-wave** within a window spanning \(R_{\text{peak}} - 250\text{ms}\) to \(R_{\text{peak}} - 50\text{ms}\).
4. **Zero-Crossing Identification:** Within these isolated windows, find where \(y'[n]\) crosses zero (changing signs). A positive-to-negative crossing denotes a standard upward wave peak.

Approach B: Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) Delineation

_The gold standard for production accuracy, highly resilient against sensor noise, optimized via libraries like NeuroKit2 or SciPy._

1. **Wavelet Decomposition:** Decompose the incoming 3-second buffer using a **Symlet (sym4)** or **Mexican Hat** wavelet across multiple frequency scales.
2. **Scale Selection:**
    - **Lower Scales (High Frequencies):** Isolates high-velocity transitions, making it easy to map QRS boundaries.
    - **Higher Scales (Low Frequencies):** Suppresses noise to highlight low-frequency, smooth profiles like P and T wave arcs.
3. **Zero-Crossing of Coefficients:** The transform converts structural boundaries into zero-crossings and maximum/minimum inflection pairings, making delineation highly stable even when the underlying baseline drifts.

Comparison Matrix

|Metric|Derivative Thresholding (Approach A)|Wavelet Transform (Approach B)|
|---|---|---|
|**Computational Cost**|Ultra-Low (Simple additions/subtractions)|Moderate to High (Matrix convolutions)|
|**Noise Immunity**|Poor (Requires pristine pre-filtering)|High (Inherent multi-scale noise rejection)|
|**Implementation Complexity**|Simple state-machine logic|High (Requires dedicated math libraries)|
|**Best Use Case**|Real-time on-device mobile processing|Desktop dashboards or cloud analytics|

---

4. Production-Grade Guardrails

To prevent movement artifacts from skewing your production analytics, implement these sequential validation constraints:

4.1 Real-Time Baseline Wander Correction

A standard Butterworth bandpass filter can cause phase distortion at lower cutoffs, artificially lengthening your intervals.

- **Correction:** Run a fast rolling median filter with a window size of 200ms to estimate baseline wander, then subtract this baseline directly from the raw incoming stream.

4.2 Physiological Boundary Verification

If an interval falls outside valid physiological parameters, the system must discard the cycle as an artifact:

- **QRS Duration:** Must fall within **60 ms to 140 ms**.
- **PR Interval:** Must fall within **120 ms to 220 ms**.
- **QT Interval:** Must fall within **300 ms to 500 ms** (subject to real-time Bazett/Fridericia heart-rate correction calculations).

4.3 Signal Quality Index (SQI) Filtering

Before processing the rolling window, calculate the standard deviation and kurtosis of the signal's first derivative. If the kurtosis drops significantly below 5, it indicates a high-noise state (e.g., sensor detachment or heavy muscle shivering). The system should temporarily freeze interval updates and display a "High Noise Calibration" alert to the user.

Would you like a functional boilerplate code template implementing the **Approach A (Derivative State Machine)** or **Approach B (Wavelet Transform)**, and if so, in which **programming language** (e.g., Python, Kotlin, Swift, or C#) should it be written?

heading_path: Activity, Sedentary Time, and Behavior Change > Synthesis
content:
Activity and sedentary behavior are the most evidence-supported places to begin. Reviews and meta-analyses consistently suggest wearable activity trackers can increase physical activity, especially when they provide self-monitoring, feedback, goal setting, prompts, and review loops rather than passive tracking alone [S01](../sources/bibliography.md#s01-ferguson-et-al-2022), [S02](../sources/bibliography.md#s02-tang-et-al-2020), [S03](../sources/bibliography.md#s03-brickwood-et-al-2019), [S04](../sources/bibliography.md#s04-chia-et-al-2019).

For everyday users, the useful longitudinal analysis is not simply "steps today." It is a multi-scale view of movement patterns:

- Daily movement dose: steps, active minutes, and estimated moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.
- Weekly distribution: whether movement is concentrated in one or two days or distributed across the week.
- Sedentary fragmentation: number and duration of long inactive bouts.
- Habit windows: times of day when the user reliably moves or tends to be sedentary.
- Progress relative to the user's baseline and chosen goal, not only public-health thresholds.

heading_path: Activity, Sedentary Time, and Behavior Change > Candidate User Metrics
content:
| Metric | Definition | User Interpretation | Suggested Guardrail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Movement dose | Weighted blend of steps, active minutes, and workouts | "How much useful movement did I accumulate?" | Avoid implying exact calories or exact fitness effect |
| Consistency score | Percentage of days meeting a personalized minimum movement floor | "Am I keeping the habit alive?" | Do not punish rest days; allow training/recovery context |
| Sedentary streaks | Count and duration of prolonged inactive bouts | "Where can I break up long sitting?" | Only use posture-specific language if posture is measured |
| Best movement window | Time periods where activity most often occurs | "When does movement fit my life?" | Recompute monthly to avoid stale advice |
| Weekend-weekday contrast | Difference in movement dose and sedentary time | "How does my routine change?" | Frame as pattern recognition, not judgment |
| Active-minute guideline progress | Weekly minutes above intensity threshold | "Am I approaching guideline-like activity?" | Explain that device intensity estimates are approximate |

heading_path: Activity, Sedentary Time, and Behavior Change > Study Notes and Quality Comments
content:
- Ferguson et al. [S01](../sources/bibliography.md#s01-ferguson-et-al-2022) is the strongest high-level evidence base because it is an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. It supports activity trackers as generally effective for physical activity, body composition, and fitness outcomes, but it does not specify which exact product analytics maximize engagement.
- Tang et al. [S02](../sources/bibliography.md#s02-tang-et-al-2020) focuses on healthy adults and concludes effects are modest and short-term. This matters for product design: the app should plan for novelty decay and habit maintenance.
- Chia et al. [S04](../sources/bibliography.md#s04-chia-et-al-2019) shows common tracker features map to behavior-change techniques, especially goal setting, self-monitoring, feedback, prompts/cues, and rewards. However, the device set was small and older, so use it as design logic rather than current market audit.

heading_path: Activity, Sedentary Time, and Behavior Change > Practical Implications
content:
Recommended analyses for an everyday wearable:

- **Personalized movement floor:** "On your better-feeling weeks, you usually get at least 5,500 steps or 35 active minutes on 5 days. This week: 3 of 5."
- **Movement opportunity map:** Identify two or three recurring times where short activity is realistic.
- **Sedentary recovery breaks:** Detect long inactivity bouts and nudge with low-friction actions.
- **Training load lite:** For non-athletes, summarize unusual spikes in activity that may affect recovery metrics the next day.
- **Goal calibration:** Adjust goals based on rolling baseline and recent adherence so goals remain reachable.

heading_path: Activity, Sedentary Time, and Behavior Change > Contradictions, Limitations, and Open Questions
content:
- Step count is easy to understand but incomplete. It undercounts cycling, strength training, swimming, and some occupational movement.
- Sedentary behavior is not simply "low steps"; posture-aware or context-aware sensing is better, but many wearables lack reliable posture detection.
- Wearables may increase activity in the short term, but long-term adherence is less certain.
- Social comparison can engage some users and discourage others; it should be optional and carefully framed.

heading_path: Autonomic and Recovery Metrics > Synthesis
content:
Autonomic metrics are compelling because they translate continuous physiology into a sense of recovery, strain, and readiness. The central signals are resting heart rate, HRV, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and sometimes electrodermal activity. The evidence supports their use as within-person trends and anomaly indicators, but not as simple labels such as "stressed," "recovered," or "healthy" without context [S13](../sources/bibliography.md#s13-shaffer-and-ginsberg-2017), [S14](../sources/bibliography.md#s14-baigutanova-et-al-2025), [S16](../sources/bibliography.md#s16-pinge-et-al-2024), [S17](../sources/bibliography.md#s17-hickey-et-al-2021).

HRV is especially attractive but easy to overstate. Shaffer and Ginsberg [S13](../sources/bibliography.md#s13-shaffer-and-ginsberg-2017) describe common HRV families, including time-domain metrics such as SDNN and RMSSD. In consumer wearables, nighttime or resting HRV trends are typically more defensible than arbitrary daytime HRV snapshots because motion, posture, breathing, and measurement quality can strongly affect readings.

heading_path: Autonomic and Recovery Metrics > Candidate User Metrics
content:
| Metric | Definition | User Interpretation | Suggested Guardrail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resting heart rate baseline | Rolling median nighttime/morning RHR | "Your cardio baseline is trending up/down" | RHR changes are nonspecific |
| HRV baseline | Rolling median RMSSD or device-validated HRV | "Your recovery signal is above/below your usual range" | Avoid population ranking as primary feedback |
| HRV stability | Day-to-day variation or coefficient of variation | "Your recovery has been more variable than usual" | Requires enough valid measurements |
| Overnight downshift | Drop from daytime/evening HR to sleep HR | "Did your body settle overnight?" | Can be affected by late exercise, alcohol, illness, heat |
| Respiratory/temperature deviation | Rolling baseline deviation during sleep | "Your overnight signals were unusual" | Do not diagnose infection |
| Strain-recovery response | HRV/RHR change after activity, travel, alcohol, or poor sleep tags | "How your body tends to respond" | Present as association |

heading_path: Autonomic and Recovery Metrics > Study Notes and Quality Comments
content:
- Shaffer and Ginsberg [S13](../sources/bibliography.md#s13-shaffer-and-ginsberg-2017) is a foundational HRV metrics overview, but it is not a validation of consumer devices.
- Baigutanova et al. [S14](../sources/bibliography.md#s14-baigutanova-et-al-2025) collected real-world smartwatch data from 49 healthy adults over four weeks, sampled frequently enough to compute short-term HRV features. This supports feasibility and benchmarking, not broad consumer normative claims.
- Stress detection reviews [S16](../sources/bibliography.md#s16-pinge-et-al-2024), [S17](../sources/bibliography.md#s17-hickey-et-al-2021) suggest multimodal signals such as HRV and EDA are more informative than average heart rate alone, but stress ground truth remains difficult.

heading_path: Autonomic and Recovery Metrics > Practical Implications
content:
Recommended product analyses:

- **Recovery trend, not readiness verdict:** "Your overnight HRV has been below your 60-day baseline for 3 of the last 4 nights."
- **Context-based interpretation:** Ask lightweight prompts only when useful: "Anything unusual yesterday: illness, alcohol, hard workout, travel, poor sleep, stress?"
- **Confidence gating:** Suppress HRV insights when wear time, motion artifacts, or signal quality are poor.
- **Two-layer explanation:** Show a simple statement first, then allow users to inspect the contributing signals.
- **Adaptive education:** Teach that lower HRV or higher RHR is nonspecific and best interpreted as a check-in cue.

heading_path: Autonomic and Recovery Metrics > Contradictions, Limitations, and Open Questions
content:
- HRV is affected by respiration, posture, measurement window, age, sex, fitness, medication, and disease state.
- Consumer PPG-derived HRV is not equivalent to clinical ECG-derived HRV in all conditions.
- Stress labels can be wrong or intrusive; "physiological load" or "body activation" may be more honest language.
- More evidence is needed on whether HRV feedback improves everyday wellness behavior outside athletic populations.

heading_path: Engagement, Explainability, and User Trust
content:
[Back to README](../README.md)

Related clusters: [Activity and Behavior Change](activity-and-behavior-change.md), [Personal Baselines and Anomaly Detection](personal-baselines-anomaly-detection.md), [Autonomic and Recovery Metrics](autonomic-and-recovery-metrics.md)

heading_path: Engagement, Explainability, and User Trust > Synthesis
content:
Wearable longitudinal analysis is only useful if users understand it, trust it, and can act on it without feeling judged or overwhelmed. The strongest design evidence points toward behavior-change techniques: self-monitoring, feedback, goal setting, prompts/cues, action planning, and review of goals [S04](../sources/bibliography.md#s04-chia-et-al-2019). JITAI theory adds timing and context: deliver support when the user is receptive and able to act [S05](../sources/bibliography.md#s05-hardeman-et-al-2019), [S06](../sources/bibliography.md#s06-nahum-shani-et-al-2018).

The key product challenge is to move from data display to sense-making. Everyday users need trends, explanations, and low-friction actions, not a flood of metrics.

heading_path: Engagement, Explainability, and User Trust > Candidate Engagement Analyses
content:
| Analysis | Inputs | User-Facing Use | Guardrail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Insight usefulness tracking | Views, dismissals, action taken, opt-outs | Suppress low-value insight types | Avoid manipulative engagement optimization |
| Receptivity windows | Time of day, prior prompt response, context | Time nudges when action is likely | Respect quiet hours and user control |
| Goal review loop | Goal adherence, baseline, missed days | Recalibrate goals monthly | Avoid making goals easier without transparency |
| Explanation templates | Metric contribution and confidence | Show why an insight appeared | Do not expose fake precision |
| User tags and reflection | Optional event/mood/context tags | Help users learn personal associations | Keep tagging lightweight |

heading_path: Engagement, Explainability, and User Trust > Study Notes and Quality Comments
content:
- Chia et al. [S04](../sources/bibliography.md#s04-chia-et-al-2019) found all assessed trackers used evidence-based behavior-change techniques, especially goal setting, self-monitoring, and feedback, but sedentary behavior was less consistently targeted.
- Hardeman et al. [S05](../sources/bibliography.md#s05-hardeman-et-al-2019) screened 2200 titles and included 19 papers reporting 14 JITAIs. Participants generally found JITAIs acceptable, but behavior effects were mixed and no study was sufficiently powered to detect behavior effects.
- Nahum-Shani et al. [S06](../sources/bibliography.md#s06-nahum-shani-et-al-2018) provides a conceptual architecture for JITAIs: decision points, tailoring variables, intervention options, decision rules, and proximal outcomes.

heading_path: Engagement, Explainability, and User Trust > Practical Implications
content:
Recommended product patterns:

- **Metric-to-action mapping:** Every insight should include a plausible action or reflection prompt.
- **Confidence labels:** "Strong pattern," "early pattern," and "needs more data" can reduce overinterpretation.
- **Weekly narrative summaries:** Users often need synthesis: "What changed? What stayed stable? What might be worth trying?"
- **User agency:** Allow users to mute metric categories, choose goals, and correct interpretations.
- **Minimalist default dashboard:** Prefer 3-5 core longitudinal signals rather than dozens of simultaneous charts.

heading_path: Engagement, Explainability, and User Trust > Contradictions, Limitations, and Open Questions
content:
- More engagement is not always better; compulsive checking can be counterproductive.
- JITAI effectiveness evidence is still developing, especially for long-term outcomes.
- Some users prefer quantified detail; others prefer simple coaching. The product may need adjustable depth.
- A system optimizing app opens may undermine health goals if it creates anxiety or dependency.

heading_path: Personal Baselines and Anomaly Detection
content:
[Back to README](../README.md)

Related clusters: [Autonomic and Recovery Metrics](autonomic-and-recovery-metrics.md), [Sleep and Recovery](sleep-circadian-recovery.md), [Activity and Behavior Change](activity-and-behavior-change.md)

heading_path: Personal Baselines and Anomaly Detection > Synthesis
content:
The central longitudinal advantage of a 24/7 wearable is that it can learn what is normal for one person. This is more relevant to everyday users than broad population comparisons because wearable physiology is highly individualized. A useful system should maintain personal baselines for sleep, resting heart rate, HRV, respiratory rate, temperature, activity, and inactivity, then report deviations in a calm, contextual way.

Evidence from influenza-like illness and COVID-19 research shows that changes in resting heart rate, sleep, and related wearable metrics can precede or track illness patterns [S11](../sources/bibliography.md#s11-radin-et-al-2020), [S12](../sources/bibliography.md#s12-mishra-et-al-2020). These findings justify "check-in" and "unusual pattern" experiences, but not consumer diagnosis.

heading_path: Personal Baselines and Anomaly Detection > Candidate User Metrics
content:
| Metric | Definition | User Interpretation | Suggested Guardrail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline range | Rolling median and percentile band by metric | "Your usual range" | Require stable wear history before reporting |
| Multimodal deviation | Combined unusual RHR, HRV, sleep, temp, respiration | "Several signals are outside your usual range" | Use as check-in, not disease prediction |
| Recovery-to-baseline time | Days for metrics to return after unusual event | "How long your body took to settle" | Needs event tagging or inferred event windows |
| Seasonal/routine trend | Month, weekday/weekend, and schedule patterns | "Your routine shifts by season/day type" | Avoid overfitting small histories |
| Data confidence | Wear time, signal quality, missingness | "How much should I trust today's summary?" | Hide or soften low-confidence results |

heading_path: Personal Baselines and Anomaly Detection > Study Notes and Quality Comments
content:
- Karimi et al. [S07](../sources/bibliography.md#s07-karimi-et-al-2024) analyzed heart rate and activity from 1014 smartwatch users and found recurring daily/sleep HR patterns plus seasonal and weekday/weekend differences. This supports pattern discovery as a user-facing theme.
- Radin et al. [S11](../sources/bibliography.md#s11-radin-et-al-2020) used de-identified Fitbit RHR and sleep data from 47,249 users to improve state-level influenza-like illness surveillance. This is strong evidence for population-level signal, but individual user alerts require more caution.
- Mishra et al. [S12](../sources/bibliography.md#s12-mishra-et-al-2020) showed smartwatch anomalies could identify a portion of COVID-19 cases before symptoms in retrospective analysis. This supports multimodal anomaly logic but is disease- and context-specific.

heading_path: Personal Baselines and Anomaly Detection > Practical Implications
content:
Recommended product analyses:

- **Usual-range visualization:** Replace red/yellow/green labels with "within usual range," "slightly outside," and "well outside."
- **Clustered anomaly explanation:** "Higher RHR + lower HRV + more sleep than usual" is more understandable than an opaque anomaly score.
- **Delay diagnosis language:** Use "consider checking in with how you feel" rather than "you may be sick."
- **Context learning:** Ask optional tags after anomalies and use them to improve future explanations.
- **Seasonality and weekday/weekend baselines:** A user's Saturday physiology may differ from Monday; baselines should respect routine segments.

heading_path: Personal Baselines and Anomaly Detection > Contradictions, Limitations, and Open Questions
content:
- False positives can erode trust; false negatives can create false reassurance.
- Baseline models can drift if the user changes lifestyle, job, training, sleep schedule, medication, or device.
- Population surveillance success does not imply individual diagnostic accuracy.
- Anomaly models need explicit policies for menstrual cycles, shift work, travel, illness, and low data quality.

heading_path: Sleep, Circadian Regularity, and Recovery
content:
[Back to README](../README.md)

Related clusters: [Autonomic and Recovery Metrics](autonomic-and-recovery-metrics.md), [Personal Baselines and Anomaly Detection](personal-baselines-anomaly-detection.md), [Engagement and Trust](engagement-explainability-trust.md)

heading_path: Sleep, Circadian Regularity, and Recovery > Synthesis
content:
Sleep is highly relevant for everyday health engagement, but wearable sleep metrics should be reported with the right level of humility. The evidence supports ecological, longitudinal monitoring: timing, duration, regularity, wakefulness trends, and behavioral routines. The evidence is weaker for consumer-grade fine-grained staging such as exact REM/deep sleep minutes [S08](../sources/bibliography.md#s08-guillodo-et-al-2020), [S09](../sources/bibliography.md#s09-birrer-et-al-2024), [S10](../sources/bibliography.md#s10-lee-et-al-2023).

The most useful user-facing analyses are therefore rhythm and stability analyses:

- Sleep midpoint and variability.
- Bedtime/wake-time regularity.
- Sleep opportunity vs estimated sleep obtained.
- Sleep debt/recovery trend across 7-14 days.
- Coupling between sleep and next-day physiology or activity.
- "Unusual night" detection relative to the user's own pattern.

heading_path: Sleep, Circadian Regularity, and Recovery > Candidate User Metrics
content:
| Metric | Definition | User Interpretation | Suggested Guardrail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sleep rhythm consistency | Variation in sleep onset, wake time, and midpoint | "How regular is my sleep schedule?" | Emphasize schedule patterns over moralized scoring |
| Sleep opportunity gap | Time in intended sleep window minus detected sleep | "Am I giving myself enough sleep opportunity?" | Works best with optional intended bedtime/wake target |
| Sleep continuity trend | Wake after sleep onset or movement-based awakenings | "Was sleep more interrupted than usual?" | Avoid clinical insomnia claims |
| Recovery night marker | Combined sleep duration, regularity, RHR, HRV | "Did last night look restorative for me?" | Label as estimate, not diagnosis |
| Social jetlag proxy | Difference in sleep midpoint between workdays and free days | "How different are my weekday and weekend rhythms?" | User schedules vary; ask about shift work |

heading_path: Sleep, Circadian Regularity, and Recovery > Study Notes and Quality Comments
content:
- Guillodo et al. [S08](../sources/bibliography.md#s08-guillodo-et-al-2020) reviewed 19 studies and found wearable sleep monitoring feasible but reliability problems compared with polysomnography. This supports using wearables for low-burden longitudinal monitoring but not clinical-grade interpretation.
- Birrer et al. [S09](../sources/bibliography.md#s09-birrer-et-al-2024) reported average sleep/wake classification accuracy around 87.2% across assessed devices and emphasized that most PPG-based sleep staging algorithms remain proprietary. It also found stronger performance for sleep/wake than multi-stage classification.
- DPSleep [S18](../sources/bibliography.md#s18-rahimi-eichi-et-al-2021) is valuable because it focuses on open, longitudinal sleep estimation from raw accelerometer data and includes quality-control logic.

heading_path: Sleep, Circadian Regularity, and Recovery > Practical Implications
content:
Recommended product analyses:

- **Weekly sleep rhythm report:** "Your wake time varied by 1h 35m this week, mostly due to Saturday and Monday."
- **Bedtime opportunity insight:** "When your sleep window starts before 11:30 PM, your sleep duration tends to be 42 minutes longer."
- **Recovery pairing:** Link sleep to next-day RHR/HRV/activity as an association: "After shorter nights, your resting heart rate has tended to run higher."
- **Stage de-emphasis:** If stages are shown, present them as rough estimates and avoid making them the main driver of recommendations.
- **Shift-work mode:** Allow users to define nonstandard sleep anchors so regularity is not unfairly scored.

heading_path: Sleep, Circadian Regularity, and Recovery > Contradictions, Limitations, and Open Questions
content:
- Consumer devices may overestimate sleep when users are motionless but awake.
- Sleep staging accuracy varies by device, firmware, population, and access to raw data.
- Some users experience anxiety from sleep scores; consider trend-based, non-punitive language.
- More research is needed on whether consumer sleep feedback improves sleep behavior or mainly increases attention to sleep.

heading_path: Search Strategy > Date and Scope
content:
Searches were conducted on August 4, 2026. The research question was scoped to longitudinal physiological analysis from 24/7 consumer or near-consumer wearable devices for everyday health engagement.

The synthesis prioritized:

- Systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
- Longitudinal empirical wearable studies.
- Sleep, HRV, activity, stress, anomaly, and behavior-change methods papers.
- Open-source GitHub repositories that help implement or interpret the analyses.

heading_path: Search Strategy > Search Surfaces
content:
- General academic web search.
- PubMed/PMC records when available.
- Publisher pages including The Lancet Digital Health, JMIR, Springer Nature, Nature/npj/Scientific Data, Frontiers, MDPI Sensors.
- GitHub repository search and repository pages.
- DOI and paper landing pages where accessible.
